div.p: LADIES' LETTER.
UT DEAREST NELLIE,

Crepon seems to hold the fororroet lace, as it has done for so long, as a. fabric for summer wear. Crocodile ciepon, as that variety is called which allows a very thick rib, is preferred to the plainer sort for a me:neut. li,eigalino and Irish poplin are favourites with both young and old, but by common consent brocades are aclooteti by married women, and glare silks by girls. Fir ceremonious occasibna, inch as webdings and garden parties, white and gold brocades are very suitable. One of thisi was made with a perfectly plain tkirt bordered with a line of bright cherry pink velvet round the hem, and with the bodice much trimmed with folds of cherry-pink chiffon, velvet in the same tint being folded round toe collar. Another pale brocade, white shot wi' II mauve and green, and strewn over with small single flowers, was finished at the shoulders with a yoke of pale green velvet, the ptiffa of the sleeves being in the same material. Almost any serge coirume may be called suitable for boating or pitching, provided it has a touch of white about ii here awl there, is embroidered with a sufficient number of gold or blue anchors, and is Worn with an air which will pass for nautical. In dark blue and white, provided the combination be uncommon and effective, you will find ooth origi- nality and charm. The overdress, s'Aiave, and shonlder-frills mint be of navy blue wage.

Is a mode of orna, a dress that never gess cut of 'fashion. A putty•ooloured ben- galine skirt, worn at a smart wedding, had the bodice made of pink silk, braided over in putty colours. Ahother, the skirt of which was in sky- blue, brocade, striped with biscuit-coloured moire, had a bodies of turquoise blue silk, braided in bis- cuit colour all over the back and in a straight line from the shoulder down either front. Revere graduated from the waist were faced with the same brocade as that from wnich the skirt had been out. A good model for a smart gown for the seaside is to be found in a blaok-tigered fabric of mixed Bilk and wool, the Alin muoh gored and trimmed with three bias bands of black moire. The bodice is made of black satin, covered with the, cream - coloured guipure lace, and turned back in front with bold revers, faced with white satin covered with the lace. A smart bodice which would serve for day or evening wear is in black cnifion pointed on the bust, the square yoke formed of lace and jet, as is also the lower portion of tho sleeve, while the upper has two lace frills. It is high in the throat, and ends beneath a ribbon bend.

Here are direction. for making a pretty summer bonnet of jet and roses. The shape is pointed, with lace Grown, and three jet bands. Place in front two pink roses with short stalks, which should first be fastened' together with wire, a but. barfly bow of moire at the back, two jet wings in front of it, and three more small roses resting on the hair behind. An eighth of a yard, out oa the bias, would be required to make the bow. Cut this Into four pieces, the pointed shape (it is best to out it in paper first) and two pieces of, bleak lining muslin in exactly the same shape; join two pieces with one of muslin neatly together on the wrong side, leaving the blttom loose, then turn carefully right side outwards, smooth the bow with the finders, and it is ready for sewing on. Make one pleat at the bottom when stitching the wing on, as this causes it to set properly. The two wings need net be joined together, tat are sewn on separately. The jet ornament is next sewn on, and the roses last of all. A Marie Stuart bonnet of fancy basket straw has an edging of geranium velvet. The

crown is pierced with two amber-headed pins, and two clusters of rioh velvet geraniums, in a large -size, break the outline of a small wreath of mignonette. A little Dutoh model of white moire, dotted over mod edged with Lick sequins, bad a becoming rouleau of black velvet resting on the hair. Bunches of black and white violets on either aide of th.) flout, a jecte I aigrette and loops of black velvet at the back, formed the trimming. Yours lovingly, J Emu&

Kissing as a Sanitary Sin. ;Johannes Secundus, in his " Basia," might be thought to have dealt with kissing from every conceivalle point of view, but he lived in prehygienic days, before the leai of the übiquitous bacillus had eclipsed the gaiety 0, u ,tons. Preachers of asceticsm used to condemn kis,- ing on the ground of its danger to the soul, but to the 'average sects ual man "the added spice of sin probably rmale it all more delightful. Now the apostle of sanitary perfection - is, says " The British Medical Journal,' eenouncing kissing for its danger to the body. "I la, Japanese, he tells us, are a livgir nically-mineed people, .ad they never • kiss. The Sanitary Committee of the Orange (New Jersey) Board of ileaitu has recommended that a circular be sent out to all whom it may concero " urging everyone to desist as much as possible irorn kissing, as the touching of lips is lik€ly to convey con- tagion ." That foul and deadly disease may be, and mten is,,propagatedin this way is, of course, a fact as to which there can ve no sort of doubt. Many -a mother has, like the Princess Alice, caught infection from the lis of her child eying or •dead of. diphtheria. .There is every reason to believe that the seeds of tuberculous may be imp muted by kissing, and the too common beslobbernig 01 children by friends or the family and by effusive strati gers unot be too strongly condemned on hygienic grounds. It cannot, therefore, be denied that kissing is dangerous, • but will " Sanitary Committees be able to put it dowri,as a too sanguine magistrate once undertook to "out down " suicide? Will love-making be conducted on anti-septic priiici pies ? " Kissing goes by favour" we ate, told—is it for the future to he by fawn' of the county council ? Grea-soro doubt, is Ilmica, but we will back- human nature with some confidence against her.

Scarlet Fever, Scatlatina, is an infectbus malady characterised by a peculiar eunctilez m eruption attended by sore tit roat and tebrile disturbance. the incubation Period of the aisease varies Item about 24 hours to 6 or 8 days. The invasion is usuAily mat keit by shivering, headache, often vomiting, and soreness et thre.at. On the second day of the illness the rash appears, usually !loon the chest first, but soon becemitig generails diffused. The rash is " fully ut "on the third or Lurtte ay, and then begins to fade ; when it has di cappeared, the skin commences to desquamate, the cuticle separat- ing, in scaly flak es, which ale most prominently devet oped an the palms ot the hands and soles of the feet. the temperature is usually markedly raised on the first day of the disease, and the patient remains in a feverish Co ndition during the devele pment of the rash ; the pulse is much accelerated .also euting this period. In corn- instances the disease assunns quite a mild term. scarlatina simplex; inethers the throat is markedly involved, scar (atina,anginssa. and a couttiion of diph- theritic intlarn tusteon ma) he present. The severest form of scarlati pa is the malignant variety, in which death sometimes occurs before t tw rash has had time te develop. There are severai a. que'se of scarier-fever, to which reference Must be matte. Cer.jurectivitis, otitis, and rhinitis may be present. '[here is sometimes rheu- matic mischief, and tufletr mat ion of the Bestow, mem- branes may cc cur. The meest important sequela of the disease is albu minutia, asse•cisted with involvement ot the kidneys. If these area t s are seriously affected.there is marked dropsy, and a temente conditien may super- vene. Scarlet-fever usuall affects young children, and second attacks of the dista-e' are rare. "She can't get out of this, Mrs. Bittly," he said, 'except by one way." "And that way is a marriage with my lord," de- clared the woman quickly. "You see yourself, Mr. Haskins, that I am followingout his lordship's instructions. Treat her like a lady,' says my lord, but keep her closely, and even be harsh with her; bat the moment she yields send me a line to London.' I will carry out his orders faithful. The young lady shall be kept a close prisoner here until she consents to become his lordship's wife." With these words Mrs. Bittly set down her can- tile. and withdrew abruptly, preceeded by Lora aolowe's valet. The next moment the key rattlea in the lock and was withdrawn, and Giralda. heard
her enemies descending the stairs. And then a realization of her situation came over

her soul with appalling force Imprisoned and helpless, when her lather was in danger, and a storm of terror and disgrace was im- pending over all her loved ones I "If I could only warn them I" she moaned, in a sudden wild abandonment. "If mamma could only be placed on her guard If papa had only time to escape I Oh I what shall Ido ?', She flew to the windows, and succeeded in rais- ing them. She pushed open the ltoard shutters and stared through the bars into the clear, mild night. She shook the bars with her little clenched hands; but she might as well have tried to beat out a section of the solid atone wall. She realized the fact at last with a little wail of anguish and despair, and sat down, pallid, trem- bling and frightened. "Oh, papa ! oh, mamma I" she moiled, wring- ing her hand in utter frenzy. "Who will warn you of your peril? Who will save you ? " Too excited to sit still, she arose again and hur- ried across the fluor, back and forth, like a caged leopardess. "I might have saved them !" she said, in a faltering voice, after a brief silence, broken only by the loud dashing of the waves against the rocks. "I might have made terms with Lord Ad- lowe ! If I had promised to become his wife he would have relented towards my parents. He might even have cleared papa's name, and recon- ciled him to Lord Trevelyan I Poor Rupert I Poor little Fay ! Oh 1 if I had only consented !" She writhed in her anguish as one in bodily torture. _

"I might have sacrificed myself for thcm !" she murmured, in bitter self-reproach. "Oh! if I had only done so 1 I did not dream when I refused his lordship that a detective, hired by him, had tracked mamma to The Evergreens ! Oh I shall go wild !" She moved more swiftly to and fro, her violet eyes burning with a strange and steady glow, her cheeks glowing feverishly, and her face pale to the likeness of death. In the midst of her wildness and despair she heard the sound of retreating wheels and realised that Haskins had taken his departure. The next moment she commenced pounding on the floor with one of the heavy chairs, as a sum- mons to Mrs. Bittly. The woman speedily made her appearance, a little flushed and a good deal annoyed. "Well, what's wanted ?" she said shortly. "Why, if them windows an't wide open If you want 'ern open at night, Miss' I have no objec- tions, but you can't have a light too. That would make the bars plain to any boats out along the coast." "You can close the shutters, then. I will keep the light," declared Giralda. Mrs. Bittly closed the shutters, grumbling. " Have you any children, Itlrs. Bittly ?" asked G'irahla, abruptly, as the woman turned from her finished task.

"No, Miss. The plaguey little creatures 1 I hope not," was the ungracious response. "Was that what you called me up here to ask ?" "No, but I thought if you had children you would feel for me ?" said the young girl, beginning to tremble anew. "Oh, Mrs. Bittly, you have beets a daughter. You are a woman. You must have some pity in your soul for one zo distressed as I. My father is in great danger. I was on my way to warn him when Lord Adlowe pursued me and took me prisoner ! Let me go on to my home, and I will bless you all my days ! I will remember you in every prayer so long as I live I never harmed you. I never harmed anybody. Oh, do let me go, Mrs. Bittly 1• See !" she added, eagerly. " I can pay you!" She exhibited the jewelled watch at her belt, the brooch at her throat, the buttons at her wrists, with a pathetic eagerness. " I have got some money, too !" she exclaimed. "Mamma gave me a little pocket-book in London, which I have not opened. There must be a hundred pounds in it. You shall have that, too. Say you will let me go. I can walk to Trevelyan station. Only give me my freedom 1" Mrs. Bittly gave a greedy look at the articles offered in exchange for the young girl's freedom, but she shook her head in token of refusal. • "Can nothing move you? " pleaded the maiden, catching in her own the woman's muscular, horny, hand. "Will you refuse my prayers and my bless- ings' as well as the money and trinkets?" Mrs. Bittly drew her hand away roughly. "I can't, and that's the end of it!" she said, harshly. "I'd like the money and jewelry well enough. I don't deny that. But I shall get more money by being true to my lord. And besides, I was his nurse, and I won't go back on him I" "But I will pay you more than he can ?" urged Giralda, persuasively. "Mamma is rich. She will pay you your own price, if you will set me free in time to warn papa. You can go to London with me, and not once lose sight of me until you receive your money." The woman began to grow angry. Giralda's offers appealed to her greed, and had her employer been other than Adlowe she would have broken faith with him. The conflict between her love for the profligate lord and her love of money aroused all the bitterness of her nature. "I will not !" she ejaculated. "Let this bathe end of such talk, Miss.'. The - brightness and eagerness faded from Giralda's face as suddenly as they had appeared there. "One word more," she said. "You can go with me to my home, and let me warn papa, and I will then return with you. I pledge my honour--" The woman interrupted her with a boisterous laugh. "That looks likely 1" she cried. "But even it you were willing to come back with me, your pa wouldn't let you. lila quite a fool, Miss. You've said. enough. Now gt, to sleep. I hear my old mau coining. He an't a pleasant fellow to deal with, especially when he emles home drunk from Little Grosvenor." She turned and departed, ciosing and locking the door behind her. "Site has a heart harder than stone !" thought poor Giralda. "But I will not give up yet! I cannot give up, all hope of escape while papa is in such danger !' She eat down, striving to think calmly. Her father's peril, her mother's anguish and impending disgrace, her brothers' grief and despair, the buttering of the proud Earl of Hampton—all passed in a swift but vivid review before her. She thought, too, of what trouble her own disappear- ance would 'occasion to those she loved, and her hurt grew faint and sick under its heavy and ie:.r7nl burdens. The candle was burning low Its flare gave the maiden an idea. Ws it not possitie tr. burn the weocien bars or the windows and effect her escape by lowering herself to the ground? 'rile project was scarcely conceived before it was dissipated by the deep, hoarse bark of a savage watch-dog under her garden window. Giralda sank hack benumbed and almost stupe- iie The candle burnt itself out, and the room be- came deively dark. The maiden roused herself at last, and made her way to the window that looked on the sea, and softly undid the shutters. Then situ leaned her pale face against the liars, and 14eked iipward toward the moonlit heavens. A minute later, her gaze, iowering itself, rested upon the far-up and towering walls of the Eagle's Eyrie as it stood up strongly outlined against the cie4r night sky. Bright lights streamed from the wide, uncurtained window, of its drawing-room far • down on the rocks below, mocking the maiden ith their cheerful, pleasant gleam. And from a nroodficent oriel window which overhung the sea --tor the Eyrie was perched on the very edge of the dizzy cliff—a red light streamed out. sending

tong red rays out over the restless, white-cappel waves, and looking like a beacon of safety. "It is a signal—a beason," thought Giralcla, her thoughts momentarily drawn from herself. "Can Lord Grosvenor be out on the sea to-night?" She turned her glances seaward. The next moment she caught the glimmer of white sail on the dusky waters in the distance. Straining her vision, she saw that it was a small boat sailing leisurely in the soft moonlight and starlight, among the dreamy shadows. A single figure was perceptible in the stern of the boat. It was too far away for the figure to be recog- nized, but Girabla's heart leaped and her soul was stirred with the conviction that it was the figure of her gallant young rescuer of the morning. It was not yet ten o'clock, and the idea was more than probable. A wild hope sprang to life in Giralda.'s soul. She fluttered against the bars like a frightened bird ; she waved her handkerchief at arm's length outside the window. She would have called to him, but that she dared not. The boat came nearer and nearer, its occupant all unconscious of her signals, her hopes, and her distress. She could see now that it was a trim. built pleasure boat. A little later she coula see its occupant reclining idly on the cushions in its stern, apparently wrapped in musings, as he watched the phosphorescent gleams of the uneasy waters. " It is he ! it is he !" she murmured, a sudden faintness creeping over her. "It is the young Lord Grosvenor." As if to confirm her words, the boatman removed his hat and wound his .fingers through his hair. She had noticed the same action in the morning in the young Lord of Grosvenor. And the slender figure, the fair golden hair, the clear-cut features, now in profile—Giralda fancied she recognised theta _ _

"If he would only look 1" she murmured. She fluttered her handkerchief, and waved her arm wildly through the bars. Still he did not look. His boat drifted nearer and nearer, yet still she could not have made him hear her speak without Also arousing her jailers. The wind tugged at her handkerchief. A sudden idea occurred to Giralda. She let go the bit of cambric and lace, and it flut- tered away, in fantastic little whirls at first, then in a straight line and more rapidly, all the while gradually descending, until it fluttered past the boatman, and so near that it startled him from his reverie, falling upon the water not a yard from him. He stretched out his hand and seized it. Then he examined it, and looked Up at the bluff cot-

tae. It was indeed Lord Grosvenor. The moonlight fell on his fair, boyish face, lighting it up with a peculiar beauty. With a sob rising in her throat and almost chok- ing her, thrilling all over with an irrepressible excitement, Giro,lda thrust out her arm, waving it wildly. In a moment she had caught his attentim. Then she grasped at the bars, signifying that she was a prisoner. There was a moment or two of apparent bewilder- ment on his part, and then he seemed to compre- hend that which she had desired to convey. He stood up in his boat and looked at her while ehe repeated her expressive pantomime. Then he looked at the handkerchief, turning it carefully in his hands. The delicacy and value oi the rich lace and cambric seemed to strike him as singular, as proceeding from a fisherman's cottage. He scrutinised the corners closely. Suddenly he started in wild amaze. It was evi- dent that he had detected the delicately written
name "Giralda " in the corner. He thrust the handkerchief into his breast, bowed, and waved his arms with an excitement equal to her own, and then sprang to his sail.

'The boat came nearer. - "lie recognised my name 1" cried the girl in a whirl of joy and relief. "He knows me as the lady he met this morning. He is coming nearer! He will save me! Oh, God! I pray that my rescue may not come too late for those I love !"

div.head: DOUBLE LIFE; OR, THE HAMPTON MYSTERY. – By the Author of " DABIEWOOD."
div.p: THE DOUBLE LIFE; OR, THE HAMPTON MYSTERY. - By the Author of " DABIEWOOD."

CHAPTER XXVII. • GLEAM OF LIGHT IN A DARK PLACA. How disappointment tracks The steps of hope I Miss LANDON. The house which had been chosen for the enforced asylum of Giralda, and the light from whose win- dows had been pointed out to her by Haskins, stood, as we have said, upon the summit of a bluff which rose more or less steeply from the sea. The bluff was not so high or large as that upon which the Eagle Eyrie was perched, and we.s separated from the latter bluff only by the long, wide valley, or plateau, in which nestled the hamlet of Little Grosvenor.

There was but one approach to the dwelling, and that was the rugged mountain path by which Giralda and her captor were ascending. On two sides were only rocks and chasms; on the third the sea. A more inaccesible tetreat could not have

been found upon any coast of the kingdom. The house was small in size, and rudely built of rough stones. It had a hard, weather-beaten look, but, like many of the Welsh mountain cottages, was not devoid of picturesqueness. A small, half- sterile garden lay in its rear, now mostly given up to straggling weeds. As the travellers drew near this desolate place the sound of wheels aroused some one within the dwelling. The door opened, and a woman stood on the threshold, holding at arm's length above her

head a flaring candle. At eight of this woman Ciralda's hopes revived. Surely, she thought, no woman would contribute to the misery and misfortune of one of her own sex. She resolved to appeal to her for release as soon as

Haskins should I:a-ye gone away. "Who is it?' asked the woman, in a harsh and grating voice, moving the •candle so that its rays fell in every direction. "It's me—Haskins--with the young lady," was the cautiously uttered response. "Come on, then. It's all right. My old man's gone down to Little Grosvenor. I'm all alone." Haskins hurried his ponies up to the rude porch, where they halted, tired with the recent rough ascent, while he proceeded to undo the bonds of Giralda.

" "Tied, eh ?" ejaculated the woman, holding the light for the valet's benefit. "Spunky, is she? You've brought her to the right place. Bring her into the house." Giralda's fetters being by this time removed, Harkins lifted her in his arms, and carried her into the dwelling, the woman leading and lighting the

way. The cottage possessed but four rooms, two below and two above. These rooms were of moderate size, the largest, however, being sitting-room and kitchen in one. It was to this apartment Giralda was carried.

Haskins deposited her gently enough in a rude, rush-bottomed chair, with a tall, screen-like back, before an open fireplace, where a low fire of drift- wood was burning. The room was cheaply and simply furnished with a deal table and chairs, and a little open cupboard of crockery, but, although everything was neat, there was no attempt at refinement, or even comfort. The windows were uncurtained, rude board shutters on the outside being their only screen, and these were not now closed. The woman set down her candle on a rude shelf against the chimney, and proceeded to close the shutters, after which she approached the maiden, pausing in front of her, and staring at her with undisguised curiosity. Giralda.'s heart sank again as she regarded the woman narrowly. She was long past middle age, tall and strong, and active as a sailor, with a muscular develop- ment of chest and arm many a man might envy. Her hair was grizzled, and was combed back into a little, hard knot. Her face was hard as stone in its expres,ion. There was no feminine softness nor gentleness about her. Grim and cold and hard in her natuie, she looked incapable of pity or mercy. She was the wife of a fisherman, who added that of wrecker to his legitimate occupation. The eourle were not in excellent repute among their humble neighbours' and dwelt along on the bluff, eeldom troubled by visitors. No more secluded prison for Giralda could have been devised, The selection of jailers was equally good— judging from Lord Adlowe's point of view. The woman, Mrs. Bittly, had been his lordship's nurse in his infancy, and what little heart she had was entirely devoted to her former nurseling. He had been kind to her at various periods since he had attained to manhood, and she owed the possession of her present home to his generosity—or, rather, to his weariness of her importunities. After his interview in the garden of the Park that day with Giralda, while still smarting under her rejection of his suit, Lord Adlowe had thought of his old nurse with a sense of exultation. It was Important to his plans that Giralda should leave Trevelyan Park at once. He could not risk, by her remaining there, the undoing of his life of scheming and falsifying. It was necessary that she should leave Lord Trevelyan's protection with apparent clandestine haste. It was also necessary to his purpose that she should not be permitted W return to her home, or to warn either of her parents of the danger threatening them. Deter- mined to make her his wife—since the Lady lteatrice was of course and forever lost to him— slid thus compel Giralda to become the support sad prop of his sinking fortunes, he had decided to immure her in some secluded spot until she should consent to become his wife. Acting upon this determination, he had ridden over to the bluff cottage, accompanied by Haskins, ;soon after his morning interview with Giralda. Be had renewed his acquaintance with his old :nurse, and had divulged a portion of his plans to her, enough to secure her hearty and intelligent co- operation with him. The promise of a liberal reward in the event of the success of his schemes had given a new impulse to her old affection for him, and she was prepared to carry out his inetruo- Cons with willingness and fidelity. Giralda finished her survey of the woman with a deep sigh. She saw plainly enough that her jailer entertained no friendly nor pitying senti- ments towards her, and her despair began to deepen into a sense of forlornness and desolation that was almost prostrating. "Is the oung lady's room ready, Mrs. Biter?" asked HI,. ,zins, declining the chair proffered him. "Al' dy," replied the woman, briskly. "I had just a led it when I heard your wheels. If you'll r' a,t young .ady, Mr. Haskins, we go up G tad& arose, Haskins keeping a tight grip of her a In, and Mrs. Bittly threw open a door in the wait. iisclosing a narrow, winding staircase leading to tee upper floor. • Giralda swept one wi: I 2 ance around her. Flight was Impossible. She 4.,0u1d only submit to follow her jailer quietly. Mrs. Bittly led the way up stairs to a narrow upper landing, and held the candle so that its ray fell upon the ascending pair. There was a door upon either sided the landing. That upon the right had a key in its lock. Mrs. Bittly opened this door. and conducted Giralda and her enemy into me "You see thieroom is safcenougn, Mr. Haskins,* remarked the woman, waving her .candle above her heed. "I would defy a man to get out of here, much more a delicate young lady. You can see that I and my old man havo been busy since you were here to-day !" Certainly the room had the look of a strong prison. There were two windows, one looking on the sea, and the other upon the garden, but both by order of Lord Adlowe had been provided with heavy wooden bars, spiked securely to the min- dow casings. In addition to the bars there were wooden shutters outside the sash, which could be opened or closed at will, hut which were now closed. The room was very neat and clean in all its ap- pointments. The floor had bean freshly scoured with sand. There was a table, two chairs, and a low, rude bedstead, draped with ~:oarse but clean homespun linen. Excepting toilet appurtenances, there was nothing more. Haskins deposited Giraltla's stv.wl and travel ling-bag on the table, and bestowed a glance ce approval around him.

div.head: CHAPTER XXVIII. TRACKED! Man's life is all a mist, and in the dark Our fortunes meet us, If fate be not, then what can we foresee? And how can we avoid it, if it be?
div.p: CHAPTER XXVIII. TRACKED! Man's life is all a mist, and in the dark Our fortunes meet us, If fate be not, then what can we foresee? And how can we avoid it, if it be?
DRYDEN.

Lord Adlowe paused a few moments, by the gap In the Park wall, and gazed after the waggon in which Giralda sat bound, a helpless prisoner, as Haskins drove briskly on his way toward the bluff cottage. Then the scheming profligate entered the Park grouuds, and strode briskly up to the mansion.

He sauntered into the drawing-room with a leisurely air, and sat down by the table in the chair he had before occupied. The marquis was still seated before the fire, but he turned around with an uneasy look at the entrance of his nephew. "Strange 1 this sudden illness of Giralda 1" said the old lord, with a stifled sigh, his black eyes gathering gloom. "Poor child 1 There. can, of course, be no impropriety in my going up to see her 1 I am old enough to be her grandfather. She may need a doctor—" " Nonsense, Uncle Trevclyan 1" laughed Lard Adlowe. "Your adopted niece is probably home- sick—nothing more I' The Marquis looked still more disquieted. "Homesick I" he repeated, with a sorrowful Intonation. "Perhaps so. She has been used to a gay, bright home. Yet she has seemed happy at the Park. She certainly loves me. Ormond, lam going up to her. If she is ill, her mother must be sent for. If she is sad, I will coax back her smiles! " He reached out for his staff, arose, and proceeded slowly towards the door. At the threshold be paused, his face growing sud- denly stern, as a thought flashed through his mind. "I am glad you are called back to town to-night, Ormond," he said, bluntly. . " Giralda has been cautioned against you, and she may be staying up- stairs till you are gone 1" Without waiting for a reply be passed out, and ascended the stairs, proceeding to Giralda's door, at which he knocked softly. Of course there was no response. He knocked again. "She may have fallen asleep," he muttered. "She may have fainted 1" and his uneasiness deepened into a positive trouble. He hesitated a moment, and then gently opened , the door and stepped into the room—the room of Geoffrey Trevelyaa., which he had not entered for eighteen years! The fire was burning pleasantly on the broad hearth. The wax candles were lighted in their silver sconces on the tall mantel-shelf. The luxu- rious white covered easy-chair was drawn up before the fender. The whole aspect of the room was pleasant, peaceful, and inviting. -

Lord Trevelyan saw at a glance that Glralda was not there. The pretty bed in the alcove, its white curtains looped away with ribbons, was tenant- less. "She must have got lonely and gone to the housekeeper's room," thought the marquis. "What a pretty place is the chamiaer of a pure young girl. I seem to feel Giralda's pare presence all around me. Flowers and books and pictures 1 Ab I"

He uttered that exclamation as if wounded in a vital part. His roving glance had rested upon the pictured face of Geoffry Trevelyan—that fair, boyish, innocent face, with its wonderful violet eyes so like Giralda's.
_ He sank down in a chair by Giralda's writing. table and gazed at the picture, his ruddy face al- most as white as snow.

He had seen no pieture of Geoffrey since the day be had expelled the youth from the Park under a cloud of shame and disgrace. This pictured face seemed almost like the living face of his lost Geoffrey. A flood of tender memories swept over the old man's soul in a warm and living tide, driv- ing before it all the coldness and ice of his long hatred. He put his hand to his heart with a quiver- ing groan, still keeping his gaze fixed on those blue, fearless, loving eyes. "My poor boy I" he murmured, in a broken whis- per, his black eyes moistening strangely. "My in- nocent, loving boy 1 How I loved him 1" He continued to gaze at the picture as a man dying in Eartem deserts of thirst might gaze at the far-off palm irees that denote an oasis and living springs which he has not strength to reach. "It doesn't seem credible that that face could bide a soul as black as a demon's!" he muttered, still in that strange whisper. "It .does .not spern

possinie that the neart beneath teat angol exterior could harbour thoughts of theft and murder, and basest treachery and ingratitude 1 Yet Lucifer was an angel of dazzling beauty! My poor lost Geoffref I How strangely Giralda resembles him Could Adlowe's syspiciyns of her paternity have a foundation in the truth?" He was seized with a sudden fit of trembling, his Colossal figure shaking as with an ague. He reached out his hand, clutching the writing- desk for support. His fingers brushed against the letter Giralda had written to him... He lifted
it idly, a smile traversing the gloom of his connten.

ance. The little angel!" he thought, fondly. "She has been writing to her mother, and has forgotten to stamp her letter." He glanced at the address, started, and tore it open nervously. He read it, the smile frozen on his lips. "Gone! gone 1" he said, hollowly. "She has left me! And I loved her so! What is there abou4; me that all whom I love are untrue to me, or forsake me? Oh, Giraldal I would have died for you 1" He laid his grand old bead down on her desk, andisobbed aloud. He had not experienced such

emotion for eighteen years—not since the great shadow had fallen on his life. And now it seemed as it had seemed then, as if the great deeps of his soul were broken up. "She has deserted me!" he thought. "She is tired of the grumbling old fellow who loves her so. Oh, my darling I my darling 1" and his whole frame was racked with his bitter, tearing grief. "Yet she does love me 1" he added, "She says so in her letter. She is in great trouble. Ormond admired her. Can he have pestered her with pro- fessions of love? By heaven, if he has, he will regret it !" He checked his sobs and sat up. He noticed that his gifts to her were all there, and that the trunk which had arrived for her from home that
morning had apparently not been unpacked. The arrival of that trunk was evidence that she had not been summoned home. She had been gay and _ _ _ _
joyous enough when she set oil on her ride with Zatinie. He had not seen her since, but it was

evident that some trouble had fallen upon her, or that she had Le n seiv-d with an uncontrollable homesickness. His suspicions pointed to the former theory, and to Lord Adlowe as the author of thot trouble.

"She has started for home, as she says," be soli!oquised. "She must have started since night- fall, and be en her way on foot and in this darkness to Trevelyan station. I must go in search of her at once."
He put the letter in his bosom and hurried down- stairs briskly, his gout forgotten in his excitement and troutle.
In the hall he encountered a servant to whom he gave an order to have the chariot got ready at once, and he then re-entered the drawing-room.
kilowe looked up at his entrance with a half- euppressed yawn. "Well," he said, with assumed lightness, " your adopted neice ill, or merely home sick, my lord ?''

hat have yon been saying to her to-day, Adlowe 2" demanded the marquis, sternly. The profligate started and coloured. "I?" he ejaculated. Who says I have been say- ing anything to her 2" "I do I" declared the marquis. know what you have said." ' Adlowe hesitated. He was acting a part now, and meant to act it well. "All I know of the young lady's proceedings to- day is this." he said, after a brief silence. "I was in the garden when she entered it. in her riding habit, after her ride with Galilee. bhe was loosing very beautiful, and I told her so. I admired her extremely. In fact, my heart was touched. I told her so, and asked her to become my wife. She refused me, and returned to the house. Bat surely our brief interview cannot have made her ill. She did not tell you that I was not most respectful and considerate. The eagle eyes of the marquis strove to pierce his nephew's soul. He was not half satisfied with Adlowe's explanation, and his dissatisfaction appeared in his gloomy eyes and knitted brows. "You have driven her from me 1" he exclaimed, with a savage vehemence, blazing lights shooting Out. i:ual tee gloi,ei ut nia eyes. " 6ne is gone The only creature I love in the world has left me! I warned you to let her alone—poor, innocent, persecuted little one. Now understand me, Ormond, Lord Adlowe. These estates are mine whi.e I live. I shall claim my rights to the utter- most points of the law, and close the doors of Trevelyan Park against you during my lifetime, unless you assist me in finding Giralda, and, when she is found, make to her such apologies and explanations as shall cause her to return to me. You hear me 7" "I hear," was the quiet response. "I will en- deavour to obey you, Uncle Trevelyan. lam sure. that in offering an honourable marriage to Miss ArevAo I had no intention of offending her and driving her from the Park." "That may or may not be so," said the old lord, with a cynical smile. "I think, however, that you speak truthfully. Giralda, with her neat little fortune and her wonderful beauty, would not be a bad speculation for you," ~,nd he sneered, "es- pecially since you must begin to see that the Lady Beatrice Hampton doesn't care two straws for you and has been playing with you all these years. But get ready. The chariot will soon be at the door.' He rang for Wigby, and ordered his overcoat and mufflers. He was dressed and impatient to be gone long before the chariot was announced. Ad- lowe was also leady and equipped for his journey to London. " Now drive like the furies 1 " commanded his lordship addressing the coachman as be paused, his hand on the door of the vehicle. "But mind and stop at sight of the first person by the road- side." He made a dive into the interior of the chariot, Lord Adlowe following. "Where's that villain of yours, Ormond I" he inquired, leaning back, as the vehicle started. down the avenue. "That Haskins, I mean, with a strangely familiar face and unfamiliar name r "He is over at the station. I sent him in ad- vance," was the careless reply. " Humph I Well, here we go! Now keep a good look-out, Adlowe, if you want me ever to treat you deoently again. Find Giralda for me and I'll pay your debts for you, and think you axe not so bad as you seem 1" The lumbering old chariot rolled on down the avenue, eliciting groans from the marquis now and then, as his gouty foot was jarred, and frequent curses from the Sybaritic profligate. NO sign of Giralda was seen on the road leading to the village. Regardless of his pains, Lord Tre- velyan kept up a constant watch from either win- dow, with the eyes of a lynx, which nothing escaped. He ordered a step once or twice at some roadside bush or stone, in the shadow of which he fancied a woman was sitting; but of course, his search was vain. On reaching the station Adlowe booked himself for his journey, while Lord Trevelyan made urgent Inquiries, went to the inn, and e von looked into the shops in the hope of finding his lost darling. In vain. It was as if she had disappeared from the earth on leaving Trevelyan Park. "Where can she be 7" ejaculated the marquis, with a worn, white face, as he approached Adlowe, who had seated himself on a bench under the pro- jecting roof of the station. "There is some mystery in this which I cannot fathom. Giralda said in her letter she wa.; going home. This is the only route to her home, yet she is not here. Where is she?" "Could she have fallen off one of those awkward bridges 2" suggested Adlowe, with an appearance of concern. "The moon had not risen when she set out " "She might I" responded the marquis, with agi- tation. "I will wait here until the train goes, to see if she conies up. She may be walking about the streets to pass away the time. If Ido not find her here, I will search the road over which she must have passed I" "She may be at home, after all. It will all come out right, uncle. And there comes my train I " Adlowe started up, bustling and self-conscious. The train dashed into the station. Adlowe took his seat, and was whirled away on his journey, leaving the desolate and almost broken-hearted old lord to commence his melancholy search for his lost Ska.l44.

div.p: At the fist station at which they stopped, Ad- lowe telegraphed to Rush, the detective, to meet him at the London station. This done, he drew his coat collar around his ears, settled back in his seat, and gave himself up to thoughts in which some pleasant ones were mingled with the bitter. He arrived in London at a late, or rather early hour. Detective Rush was in waiting for him at the station, and the two proceeded by cab to Adlowe's hotel. Not a word passed between the couple conceni- ing their business until they were seated in Ad low's dreary room. Then Rush rubbed his hands and chuckled softly in appreciation of his own keenness. "The Lady Beatrice Hampton is a wonderful woman—wonderful 1" he exclaimed. "As keen as a- briar, as sharp as a razor 1 1 never met with such caution, such guardedness, in the whole coarse of my professional career l'' "Yet you telegraphed that you had tracked her to her secret retreat 2" said Adlowe, anxiously. "I did. I have. Yesterday afternoon the Lady Beatrice, with one trunk and a baz—it is well to be always exact—set out for Victoria station, ostensibly on a week's visit to the Charlcons of Charlton Place, Surrey. I followed to the station. The footman told me by judicious pumping what I have just learned. I booked myself by the same train. Her ladyship got out at Dalton, a station fifty miles down the line. I went on to the next station not to arouse her attention or suspicions, and returned by the next train. As I half ex- pected, her ladyship, with a different shawl and a heavy veil, came on this train, going back toward London. She got out at Limely ; but having freed my game, I did as before, going on to ths next station. I returned to Limely an hour later. My lady was not there, I inquired of a porter, describ- ing her ladyship. He said that a lady answering to her ladyship's deseription had got out at Limely, and that she had gone to Senor Arevalo's. Senor . Arevalo, it appears, is a Seauish gentleman, and lives at a place called The Evergreens. The Senor's pony carriage was waiting for her ladyship. I found out The Evergreens, but it is shut from the street by a high brick wall, and its gate was locked. My investigations ended at the gate. However, I took an impression of the lock, and procured a key to fit it to-day. 'Here it is!' Adlowe flushed with pleasure. "You have done well," he said, taking the key. "Your reward shall be ample. I have learned something while away, and I held in my hands the clue to all this mystery. I believe I know who this Senor Arevalo is. Did you make no inquiries about him 2" "Yes, my lord, of the tradespeople. Few people have ever seen him. He leads a very retired life, is a writer, or some such thing. His wife is a singer or actress in London. He is a grandee and eNile from Spain. That is all I learned." "Ah 1 The actress or sineer is the Lady Beatrice Hampton," said Ad:owe, with a bitter smile. "It must be an intrigue, my lord, we have not yet fathomed her lad sship's secret," said the detective, • gravely. "I have searched all the parish registers at the West End, and have found no register of her ladyship's marriage with any one. I doubt that she is redly married." Adlowe considered the question in serious earnest, beginning to hope that the connection between the Lady Beatrice and the soi-distant Count Arevalo had not the sanction of the law. Remembering her ladyship's pride and fine sense of honour and the bonosr also of his traduced and wronged cousin, he speedily dismissed this vain hope. "I discovered, as I said, front the tootman, trial her ladyship would be absent a week. She means to spend that week at The Evergreens. Your lord- ship will therefore have time to confront her there, if you chose to do so, when your lerdship is fully rested. Am Ito go any further in the mat- ter, my lord ?" added the detective, "or do my services end here 2" "I may want you further. I don't know," said Adlowe, reflectively. "But not just now. I can work up your discoveries to suit myself at my leisure. You will be in readiness to take up toy Work et any time I may require you." He enforced this view by laying down before his ally a bank-note of handsome 'dimensions. His lordship had raised money since his return to Eng- loud, in that manner so well known to British fast youth—that is, by post obits. This borrowing money on the strength of his expectations from Lord Trevelyan, and thus directly calculating on the demise of his lordship was in lull keeping with Adlow's character. The detective pocketed the money, received the compliments Adlowe hepaed upon him, and took his departpre, leaving his lordship to take - and pursue the threads he had so carefully un- ravelled. Adlowe spent the forenoon in bed. In the after- a *soon he called at the Earl of Hampton's. espressede e • els regrel at roe aosenct., or toe Lady Beatrice trona town, and drove with Lord Hampton in Hyde - Park. lie dined at his club, and soon after, half e. disguising himself in his surtout, made his way to the Victoria station, in time for a down train. He 1 o Ikea himself for Lirnely, and proceeded thither. He had carefully inquired the way of Rush to The Evergreens, and on alighting at the Limely station he took his way up the street with con- siderable assurance. It was a long walk, as Giralda had found it, between the b tit ion and The Evergreen's. Adlowe passed over the ground rapidly, and halted at last at the massive gate in the high brick wall, to which was attached a board, bearing the painted legend, "1 he Evergreens." "I'm rill right, it seems," muttered the profligate lord, fitting the key Rush had given him. " take a look in at the windows. I'll make sure be• fore Ido anyt!iing rash. lam armed—doubly armed. If this Spanish grandee' proves to be Geoffrey, we shall see hot work." He opened the gate and passed into the ehadowe of the dense evergreens. lie moved like a ghost up the densely shaded walks. He approached the house. Light gleamed from the windows. The curtains were not drawn, and only thick veils el ivy and climbing plants shaded the panes. mi- l. hushed his breath, and crept closer, closer, into the very shadows of the • vines, and peered into the drawing room window ! (To lie continued).

The appearance in the country villages of a series _,61 vans labelled "Church Association" is the latest ‘4Bvice of the squire and the parson to stem the ad- lancing tide of village democracy. They represent 411. Establishment crusade in more senses than one. ia not only against such measures as the Welsh "isestablishment Bill that the latest form of the an crusade is directed, but against that other dis- establishment of the parson and the landlord which the Parish Councils Act has introduced. Tory vans 4nd landlord vans would not in these Radical days Strike such awe into the rural mind as a van corn- 1b accredited with the name of the Church; but, Whether bearing the flag of Conservatism or the Church, they have the one common object of keep- the agricultural labourer and the village trades- an and shop-keeper in the fetters which it has Cost the Government so much labour to give them the power of shaking off.

I's result of the division on the local option I C'endment to the Mines Bill on Tuesday night was dir;,ll:rPrise to both sides. It was known that the ,;:sion would he elbse, but up to the last the pro- uers of the bill hoped to defeat the amendment sraall majirity. As a matter of fact they tlonld have done so had all the Irish members in the be°,.use voted with them. Two of the Irish mem- ko?, however, left the House without voting, while voted in the majority. A number of the Con- biPttiireS who voted for the second reading of the ".were absent, but about seven or eight voted e'soalnst the amendment. As a body, however, the itlnaervatives and Unionists in the House, includ- ThR Mr. Balfour and Mr. Chamberlain, supported it. z`Leeelne.mbers of the Government present, with the tYLlon of Mr. Morley and Mr. Burt—who were Th lie other lobby,—voted against the amendment. ere is no doubt that the advanced period of the ble'ion favoured the opponents of the bill. Certain ers who have no interest in either side ad- witted eob, ly voted for the amendment because they tut:sidered it undesirable that so important a mea- , 'e should be proceeded with in a thin House or
that the session should be prolonged for the pur- pose. Of course the adoption of the amendment is fatal to the bill.

It will be found tkat the whole of the band of Northern Liberal capitalists who have paired for party questions had, as I suspected, reserved their freedom for this division, and took care to come back and vote against the bill. Erom the tone and temper of the lobby on Tuesday night it is pain- fully obvious that the course taken as to this bill will increase the friction between the labour and advanced section of the party and the old capitalist Liberals. No serious resentment is felt at the action of Messrs. Fenwick and Wilson, who are known to represent a majority of their constituents in taking all steps to oppose the bill. But the professions of the Liberal capitalists that they approve ;he prin- ciple of the bill while voting for local option are suspected. I have heard that, the votes given are not unlikely to lead to a multiplication of three- cornered fights, with a probable loss of 01.10 or two seats.

div.head: CHILD NEGLECT AT WIDNES.
div.p: THE CHILD NEGLECT AT WIDNES.
INQUEST AND VERDICT.

Mr. S. Brighouse, county coroner, on Tuesday forenoon resumed, at the W histon Workhouse, the inquest on the body of Elizabeth Ann Mercer, aged 11 years, whose death was attributed to neglect on the part of her parents, Samuel and Ann Mercer. Both parents were present in custody, the :male prisoner being brought to the court by special sanction of the Home Secretary from Walton Jail, where he is at pre- sent undergoing a term of three months' imprisonment for neglecting the child. His wife was liberated last week,after serving a month's imprisonment far the same offence, and was re-arrestsd on a charge of causing the death of the child. Evidence given by Mary Jane Mercer, Inspector M'Ateer, of the National Society for the Pile- vention of Cruelty to Children, Alfred Wood, relieving officer, and Dr. O'Keefe (Widnes), on former occasions, was again read over. Mr. Wood, in his evidence, said that during the illness of the girl the father came to him in an intoxicated condition, and on his reporting the fact to the guardians they declined to have anything to do with the matter,and told the father he must take the consequence of his own conduct.—The Coroner re- marked that he did not approve of that course. He did not see what the guardians had to do with the d alletse criminal act of the parents. Here was a child suffering from phthisis and fitted for hospital, and the responsi- bility was with the guardians. The office of guardian was not to punish but to relieve. He would like to know how it came about that the local committee, with the medical note before thern,did not take steps to have the child removed to the hospital. Witness : The committee thought the male prisoner was using them as a tool.— The Coroner : But the child was suffering, and fit for hospital. Witneas : The child was not destitute.—The Coroner : Why not ? Witness : Because she was living with her aunt.—Police-constable Worsfold stated that the male prisoner was a drunken and dissolute man,and Dr. O'Keefe gave evidence that from the results of a post-mortern examination of the body he was of opinion that the child died from pulmonary consumption, brought on by systematic starvation for a period extend- ing over two years.—The prisoners, on being asked if they had any witnesses, called Alfred Mercer and John Mercer. The former deposed that in 1889 he kept the girl at Northwich for nine months with the view of regaining her strength, as she was very delicate. The child was always provided with suitable food.—John Mercer, 8, Barnes-st., Widnes, said the girl was always well fed as far as he knew. She seemed to suffer from a wasting disease.—The Coroner, in summing up, asked the jury not to be prejudiced by the action of the magis- trates in sending Mercer and his wife to prison. As a jury, they must be satisfied that the parents had wil- fully neglected to provide the necessaries of life, and, owing to that neglect that the child had come to its death. If they were not satisfied on that paint, be did not think they had any right to say that the parents had brought about the death.—The jury, after half an hour's deliberation, returned a verdict to the effect that the deceased died from plithisis,caused by gross neglect; but they had not sufficient evidence to show how it was set up. At a special sitting of the Widnes Police Court,held en Tuesday evening,Ann Mercer was brought up on remand charged with causing the death of her daughter, Elizabeth Ann, aged twelve years, by neglecting and starving her, on the 24th ult. Superintendent Keighley said that after the verdict of the coroner's jury that day he proposed to offer no further evidence against the accused, and the magistrate (Councillor W. W. Gossage) thereupon dis- charged her.

div.head: SAD SUICIDE AT ST. HELENS. THE "BITTER CRY" OF A DISCHARGED WORKMAN.
div.p: SAD SUICIDE AT ST. HELENS. THE "BITTER CRY" OF A DISCHARGED WORKMAN.

At St. Helens Town Hall on Monday, Mr. F. A Jones, deputy county coroner, held an inquest on the body of James Bromilow, aged thirty, a bottle- maker, residing at 30, Lyon-street, who died from the effects of drinking carbolic acid on Saturday. Mrs. Bromilow, the widow, stated that her husband was employed at glass bottle works of Messrs. Can- nington, Shaw, and Co., but was discharged about eight weeks ago. He bad worked a little since at those: works, and was workine last Tuesday. He was depend- ing on getting 103. a week which the Bottlemakers' Society allowed to members who were stopped through slackness of trade. On Saturday he saw "young Mr. Chadwick." When he got home at 'twenty minutes to twelve he walked past witness aad went to the sofa and began to cry bitterly. Witness said, "Don't take on like that." He replied, "Mr. Chadwick says he can't , conscientiously say h., discharged me through slackness of work, and lam not to have my 10s. He says it will be a warning to me in the future." Deceased further said he replied," Well, Mr. Chadwick, you will take the bread out of my poor children's mouths, for I have nothing to turn to." (Here Mrs. Bromilow cried bit- terly). He then turned to his wife and said, "There is nothing but starvation for my poor children." She said "Don't take on like that; something always turns up." He afterwards went upstairs. Witness thought he would like to read, and she was taking him a newspaper when she met him on the stairs. She smelt something strange and at once suspected he had taken something. She said, "Oh, Jim. what have you done ?" He said, "I have done it for the best for you." She said, " What- ever were you thinking of ?" He said, "It is done and can't be helped." She told the eldest child to fetch a neighbour. Be slid, " Fetch no one." She, however, called a neighbour, and sent for Dr. Donellan. Two bottles containing carbolic acid were afterwards found in the bedroom. One had been purchased from Mr. Jackson, chemist, and three-parts of the contents had been taken. Asm Mier bottle had been purchased from Mr. J. Cotton, chemist, and had not been touched. Both had been purchased that mo ruing, and were properly labelled. Everything was done that could possibly be done to bring him round, but he died at a quarter to two.
After some further evidence the jury returned a ver- dict of "Suicide whilbt of unsound mind."

div.head: ANOTHER MAN DROWNED AT WESTON
div.p: ANOTHER MAN DROWNED AT WESTON
POINT.

Still another sad death from drowning has oc- curred in the locality of Weston Point, this time in the Ship Canal, near the New Basin. The victim is James Richards, aged 23. years, and is the son of Mr. George Richards, butcher, who carries on busi- ness in South-road, Weston Point, and Percival-lane Runcorn. It is appatent that the unfortunate man,who was the captain of the hopper barge " Elli," running on the Ship Canal between Weston Point and Manchester, left his post at noon on Sunday and came ashore with the mate, Edward Tellmann. Richards went to his sisters house at Weston Point, and remained there until 2.20 when after visiting the Dock Hotel he returned to his boat which was lying in the canal. He went into the cabin with the other men but at about 3 30 he left them, without saying anything, and went above heard. Some fifteen minutes afterwards, Tellmann, the mate, went up to look for him, but eould not find him. When he reached the deck his attention was drawn by a boy to a small dog in the water which the captain had brought aboard. It was swimming about near the barge and was brought up on deck. A search was made on board for Richards but has he could not be found it was concluded that he had gone home again, or else to Widnes where previously he had ob- served it was his intention to go. At three o'clock on Monday morning Tellmann went on board, and not find- ing Richards there, he put out the lights. At breakfast time Richards had not appeared, and Tellmann decided to go to the house of Richards' sister to enquire Of his whereabouts. On reaching the house he was told that the captain had not been there since the previous after- noon. The mate began to grow apprehensive and grap- pling operations near to the boat were ordered to be made. Tellmann assisted a man named Charles Bowyer in the work, and the result of their exertions was that at about 10.30 the dead body of the captain was found between the barge and the wall just under the ladder which had been placed from the barge and the dock wall for landing purposes. This was not far from where the dog had been seen swimming the previous afternoon. The deceased was well-known, and respected by many friends.—An inquiry was conducted on Wednesday morning by Mr. J. E. Worseley, coroner, at the Dock Hotel into the circumstances attending the death of Richards. Evidence in support of the above particulars and the jury finally returned a ,terdict of "Found drowned," no evideriee having been found to account for the deceased getting into the water. The supposi- tion of many folks is that Richards was in the act of landing when he fell from the ladder, with the dog in his arms, into the water, first strikintrthie-walt.s•iNo• mark% of violence were found upon the body.

div.p: IHE EKANI iNET?, SATURDAY, AUGUST 18 1894.

INTERE-vrIM, AP RUNCORN.

At the Rancorn County Court. on Tuesday morn- ing before his Honour Jude Wynne Foulke, an aclori to recover the sum of £1 14s. 31. was brought. against James Edwards, corn mere', ant, Frodshani. by the Manchester Ship Canal Company.—Mr. Now- man, of the firm of solicitors Messrs. Grundy, Ker- shaw arid Company, Manchester, appeared for the plain- tiffs, whilst the defendant was we; professionally represented. Mr. Meadoweroft. the Runcorn agent of the Ship Canal Company was also present.—Mr. New- ' man stated that the claim represented toll on certain cram n conveyed for the defendaut over the Ship Cana! from Livorpool to Preston Brook. The rate on grain from Liverpool to Preston Brook was 6•,.. per ton includ- ing collection at Liverpool. The defendant had paid £1 53. 4d. into court and held that that sum covored every- thing that was due. The defendant did not dispute the passaae of his goods over the Canal, but contended that the Company were charging him more than they were charging other people. The 93. in dispute raised an im- portant point. Woen goods were to go from Liverpool to places more than ten miles south of Preston Brook, on other canals and _railways, the Ship Canal Company were only paid 4.. 4,1. per ton as their proportion. In other words he might say that if a man were to send goods from Liverpool through to Birmingham over the Ship Canal via Preston Brook the Company would only receive 4s. 4d. per tal as their proportion. In this case, how- ever. the defendant wanted to be charged the same terms for sending goods to Preston Brook as another sender would be charged for sending so far on a through rate to Birmingham. Mr. Newman suhmitted that it was not within his honour's jurisdiction to alter the rate. If the defendant wished this to be done he would have to go before the Railway Commissioners, who alone pos- sessed the power to alter the rates and charges of canal companies and railways. Mr. Newman termed it an undue prelefence which the defendant wished by seeking to possess the benefit of a through rate to Birmingham only as far as Preston Brook His Honour remarked that the point was, had the de- fendant consigned his goods from Liverpool upon the toll to which the company were entitled P It so, he could not alter it.—Mr.Newman answered that the de:endant had done so. Mr. John Jones, collector of rates in the employ of the Manchester Ship Canal Company at Preston Brook, de- posed to having received certain goods to the order of the defendant, the toll upon which amounted in the ag- gregate to £1 14 s.3d.,at 6s. per ton. This was the rate that had been charged by old canal companies for many years before the construction of the Ship Canal. Mr. Edwards questioned the witness at some length regarding the tolls levied upon goods passing between Liverpool, Preston Brook, and onwards and elicited the fact that the Ship Canal Company would return the dif- ference between 4s. 4d. and 63. per ton if anyone were to decide, on the goods being landed at Preston Brook.to send them forward beyond ten miles of that port. The through rate to Stoke, for instance, would be 4s. 4d.,0r to any other town beyond ten miles of Preston Brook. The defendant contended that the local traders at Preston Brook were handicapped to the extent of Is. 81. by this difference in carriage being made. The judge did not think that the defendant was right in giving expression to those words at that stage. He himself did not see any handicapping at all,and he was afraid he (defendant) would have to pay the 6s. perjton. Mr. Edwards now expressed himself prepared to pay the money,adding that it was a very simplequestion,bia it was one which affected to a considerable extent the trading classes of Preston Brook. His Honour observed that it was not for him to assign any reasons whatever for the difference in the Compa ny'a rates. The defendant would have to go elsewhere for that explanation. However, he might say that it required the use of almost as much machinery to take the goods to Preston Brook as it would to the potteries. The only difference would perhaps be that a certain amount of less waterway would be covered, and not so much wear and tare. There might also be other reasons. The defendant would have to pay the amount claimed, viz., £1 14s. 3d. Mr. Newman explained that with regard to the reasons assigned for the difference there was one—and a very important one too—which he might mention, and that was that when goods were going through to the potteries from Liverpool they were nat warehoused at Preston Brook, a work, which, when rendered necessary,caused the officials and labour ers considerable trouble. When consigned to Preston Br ook goods were, of course, ware- housed, and sometimes se mained in the warehouse for very leng thy periods. BATTLE-FEA Et.

People who have never been in battle often speculate upon the courage required by our soldiers. Many of our soldiers, however, possess fear to a considerable extent. Two veterans have lately been relating their experiences to a writer to " The Sun." One of them remarked : " Every man learns when he goes in battle for the first time that he is a coward. Most men find it out before their first fight. Quite often the man who feels most fear before the fighting begins proves to be an exceed- ingly good man under fire. begins, those who seem to have no fear in them beforehand are found to be sadly lackieg when bullets begin to buzz like bees. suppose I am not counted a craven, hut I am free to confess that I never went into a fight without being half frightened to death. Once, I remember' the first shell that passed screaming overhead on the day of the first fight threw the men into a frightful state of panic. I was as had as the others—for just an instant. Then it occurred to me that as the shell that had caused what promised to be a rout struck some five hundred yards to the rear of our line, and others were falling in the same locality, it would be far more dangerous to turn back than to ad- vance, as ordered, and I got my nerve again. Fortun- ately the lieutenants of my company kept their heads quite as well or better than I did mine, and acting all together we steadied the men and saved the company the diserace of exhibiting cowardice and perhaps break- ing up the entire line. I have no doubt that my reason- ing on the subject was all done in a second or t-vo ; for if it had not been so, it would have been too lato, when I regained common sense to prevent the men from in- glorious flight, but it seemed to me then that I devoted a lull half hour to thinking it all out." The second veteran said that he was nearly frightened to death during his first fight, and was only kept from flying from the field by a timely and really kind slap on the cheek with the flat of his captain's sword. He con- tinued : .

"In my last fight I was all upset by a little circum- stance, which, if something similar were to happen to me now, would probably, literally drive me out of my wits. We got the order to charge across a field some few acres in extent. A battery of the enemy to the left was sending grape and canister across the field. At the far side was a fence, and beyond that a few rods the enemy's infantry lay entrenched behind slight and hastily thrown up earthworks. 18 ell, we started across the open space in great style. I was not a bit " funky " not I—when we got away, though, .1 remember that I did not expect to reach the fence alive. I remember dis- tinctly that when half-way across the field, I laughed aloud at the ridiculous figure cut by a man in the rank just ahead of me, who was thrown high into the air in the midst of a cloud of dust ar.d dirt by a cannon ball that struck the ground in front of him. In time we reached the fence. I was unhurt, and had run so fast that I was one of the first to climb to the top rail. Just as I was vaulting over, a shell from a rifled cannon struck the fence at the far end, and completely demo- ralized it. The thing must have burst just under me. At any rate, I was thrown higher in the air than had been the man I laughed at. and I came down to the ground in a perfect shower of splintered rails. Mcst of my clothes were gone, and so were my 2un and the rest of my equipment; but I wasn't hurt, save that one finger had left me with my apparel and other things. But I was frightened—l was awfully frightened, and I ran faster than I ever did before or ever have since. I yelled, too, and that was how I was taken prisoner, for in my fright I didn't see that I was iunning beyond our most advanced ranks and directly toward the enemy, and I never stGpped till I had passed their line of battle and had gone far to their rear. How I escaped being killed by the shower of bullets through which I sprinted, I do not know, and cannot now understand.
ANOITLX+ cIIAMiE OF PEiI.MITTINC4 • .DRUNKENNESS. AT RUNCORN. THE ClsE DISMISSED.

At the Runcorn. Petty Sessions on Monday morn- ing before Messrs. -John Brundrit. S. Taylor, 1. Kigby, and J. Handley, James Jolley and John liiiguley were summoned for having been drunk on ti:e licensed premises of the Porefst,r's Arms. Canal- st., on the night of the 28th July, and Edward For- shaw the licensee of the house was summoned for per- mitting the offence.—Mr. MelC,inzie, solicitor, of Liver- pool, appeared for the landlord of the Forester's Arms. The defendant Jolley admitted being drunk on the nrenalses but pleaded that he had had no beer in the house. Baguley denied that hi, was drunk on the pre- mises and said that he had no beer at all before him on the night alluded to. Inspector Hicks testified that whilst on duty in Canal- st. at about, 9.45 p.m. on the 28th July in the company of Sergeant Lee and Constable Richardson he heard some men quarrelling outside of the Forester's Arms. At last one of them turned and walked down Mason-st., whilst another went into the Forester's Arms. Witness, accom- pataied by the officers referred to, went towards thel vaults and entered. They found the defendant Jolley inside,drunk, leaning against the bar and drinking some beer. Baguley who was drunk was also there and took , the vessel which contained the liquor away from Jolley and drank some, saying that it belonged to him. Wit- ness called to the landlady and asked her where her husband was, and drew her attention to the state of the ; defendants, Jolley and Baguley. Mr. Forshaw, the land. lord, then came towards them and said to Baguley "I told von to go home before. You will have no more beer.'" A man named Robinson who was present in the house, then called out saying "I paid for the beer to get them out. The landlord did not serve them, be served me."

By Mr. McKenzie: Witness said there were four men in the bar when he entered the house, Baguley and Jolley being of the number. There were only two glasses before them. One of these Jolley had in his hand drinking from it; the other was on the counter. He saw no beer supplied. The landlord had given wit- ness every assistance when he came, and put Baguley and Jolley out of the house. In answer to the Chairman, the Inspector said that Baguley was one of the men who had been previously quarrelling outside the public-house. P.S. Lee corroborated the statement made by the last witness and added that he heard the landlady say that one of the men had ordered and paid for the beer for Baguley. P.C. Richardson said he heard a noise in the Pores. ter's Arms n hen f.e passed the house at 8 45 p.m. the same night. He supported the assertions of the officers already named and said that it was in consequence of having heard the noise at 8.45 that he reported the matter to the Inspector, who decided that he Sergeant Lee and himself (witness) should visit the house. At 8.45 he saw two drunken Men outside the public-house. One of the men was Baguley, and witness saw him go into the vaults at that tune. Mr. McKenzie, for the defence, submitted that no evidence had been adduced to show that the licensee had permitted drunkenness. On the night in question two men entered the Forester's Arms and asked for beer. In consequence of the landlord not have a pumping engine he had to go downstairs into the cellar for the liquor. As he was passing along the counter towards the cellar steos Baguley and Jolley came in and asked for beer. The landlord, noticing that they were under the influence of liquor, refused them and told them they must go home. When he came upstairs the police were in the bar, and it had been stated that Jolley had picked up a glass of beer and had drunk some. It was like- wise stated that Baguley had taken the glass from Jolley and had also drank ot the contents. Mr. McKenzie, concluding, stated that there must be consent, a privity oar a sort of connivance before such a charge as that ot permitting drunkenness could be established; and such a charge had not been proved in evidence. He went on to quote the ruling of an eminent authority on licensing law, who had stated that if a drunken person had not been served with liquor by the keeper of the house whilst the former was on his premises, then the keeper could not be convicted. During the construction of the Ship Canal the defendant had conducted the house in a respectable :nanner, and it would now be very hard upon him if a conviction should be recorded against him. Edward Forshaw, the licensee of the Forester's Arms, gave evidence similar to the statement of his solicitor. Being asked by the latter if there was any beer in the bar out of which his wife could have served Jolley, whilst he (Forshaw) was in the cellar, he replied that there was "a jug of sixpenny." When he ascended the steps again, however, and looked at this jug, he could see that the liquor had not been disturbed. He had himself conducted the house two years prior to which he managed it for three years for his father. By Superintendent Atherton: He had served no beer whatever to the two defendants on that night. Mrs. Margaret Alice Forshaw, wife of tne landlord. said that whilst her husband was in the cellar she did not serve anyone with any beer. The men Jolley and Bagu- ley were not in the house longer than five minutes on the night in question, and during that time she did not serve either ef them with beer. James Jolley said he was refused beer when he entered the Forester's Arms and seeing a glass near him he took it up and drank some of the liquor. Joseph Robinson deposed to Jolley being refused beer and to the latter taking his glass and drinking some of his (Robinson's) beer. Baguley also took the glass and drank some. Witness did not say anything, thinking that he might create a bother. Be did not pay for any beer for the defendants, and the glass which he paid for was for himself alone. Being questioned by Superintend- ent Atherton he denied having told Inspector Hicks that he had paid for the beer which the men had in order to make them go. The magistrates, without retiring, fined Jolley and Baguley ss. and costs and dismissed the charge against Forshaw.

div.head: WIDNES TOWN COUNCIL.
div.p: WIDNES TOWN COUNCIL.

The monthly meeting of the Widnes Town Coun- cil was held on Tuesday afternoon, at the Widnes Town Hall. The Town-clerk reported that the continued absence of the Mayor (Alderman F. H. Gossage) through indisposition, and. Alderman Sadler (Deputy-Mayor) was elected to the chair.— The medical officer reported that there were 37 deaths within the borough during July. The death-rate was 14.8 par 1,000 of the estimated population (the same as the two previous months). l'here were 58 notifications of, infectious diseases. In the return of deaths from zymotic and other diseases from the county medical officer for the three months ending June 30th, Widnes compared favourably with the other urban districts.— The Gas and Water Committee recommended that the plans and estimates submitted by the engineer (Mr. I. Carr) for further extensions at the gas works, estimated to cost £11,502 us., be approved, and that application be made to the Local Government Board for powers to borrow the money. This scheme will increase the capa- city of the works from 1,000,000 cubic feet per diem to 1,500,000 Cubic feet per diem. The committee also re- comrivnded that, in the event of the preceding resolution being confirmed by the Council, the engineer be in- structed to proceed forthwith with the removal and re- erection of the sulphate plant at the gas works, at an estimated cost of £1,500. Alderman Warring, in mov- ing the adoption of the minutes, said the proposed ex- tension was necessary owing to the enormous increase in the consumption of gas during the current year. Councillor Singleton moved an amendment that the matter be referred back for a month ; but upon a vote being taken, it was lost by 13 votes to 6.
