IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT.
MONDAY.

In the House of Commons on Monday Mr. S. Slum and Mr. NAOROJI gave notice that on going into Com- mittee on the &is,: India Revenue Accounts they would move amendments urging that inquiry should be made into the system of government in India and the condi- tion of the people in that empire. Mr. BUCHANAN gave notice of an amendment to the effect that the Govern- ment of India should have lull liberty, if necessary, to impose duties on cotton and other goods. The Equalisation of Rates (London) Bill was read a third time, and the House went into Committee on the Railway and Canal Traffic. Bill. After discussion the bill, as amended, was ordered to be rep...rted. The House then went into Committee on the Miners' Eight Hours Bill. Sir J. PEASE moved to report progress An amendment moved by Mr. STUART WORTLEY, that the duration of the bill should be 1893, was agreed to. Mr. D. A. THOMAS moved that tire Act should not be adopted in any county unless a majority of the workmen employed were in favour of it. Mr. ROBY held that local option would be fatal to the bill. Many speeches hal- lowed, the eight-hour day and the local-option principle being discussed chiefly in relation to foreign competition Mr. ROBY moved that the question be now put ; but dis- cussion was continued. Shortly before twelve o'clock Mr. WOODS moved the closure. The Chairman withheld his assent, and left his seat at midnight, the debate on the amendment being adjourned.

The second reading of the Evicted Tenants Bill was moved in the House of Lords by Earl SPENCER, who urged upon the House the necessity of passing the measure as a remedy for a real grievance. Lord BAL- FOUR of Burleigh moved the rejection of the bill. He asserted that if it were to be allowed to pass,the tenants who had rebelled against the law would be taught to believe that they were a specially favoured class. The Duke of ARGYLL, in a lengthy and impassioned speech, supported the amendment for the rejection of the bill. After slime further discussion the debate was adjourned, on the motion of the Duke of DEVONSH IRE, and the House rose.

div.head: COTIEA. AND THE COItEANS.
div.p: COTIEA. AND THE COItEANS.

The Corean warriors are almost as primitively armed I as some of the oldest-fashioned bodies in China itself,but ' the Corean is brave enough when it comes to fighting. They have no arts and industries. " What is the use of working and making money," said a Corean. " if, when the work is done and the money made,this is taken away from you by the officials,and you are worn out for having done the work, and as poor as before, if, mind you, you are fortunate enough not to be exiled to a dis- tant province l” the angry magistrate who has enriched himself at your expense ? " The people have a care- worn, sad expression. They are quarrelsome, though, in spite of their lugubrious expression. They will get up a deadly fight for the equivalent of a farthine. Anything will make them come to blows. With one hand they catch hold of each other by the knot in which the hair of all married men is tied on the top of the head, and while a violent process of head shaking is followed by a shower of blows and scratches administered by the free hand, the lower extremities are kept busy distributing kicks which should land on the antagonist, but which, occa- sionally, in tact often, reach some innocent passer-by, as the streets of Corean cities are seldom wide enough to let three people walk abreast. Seoul. the capital ,of the, Corean kingdom, is the only city where wider , streets are found, and the main street, leading to the Royal palace, is indeed immensely wide, so much so that two rows of smaller thatched houses and shops are built in the middle of the street itself, thus forming as it were three paralled streets of one stre( t ; but these houses are removed and pulled down two or three times a year ' when his Majestk the King chooses to come out of his palace and goes in his state chair either to visit the tombs of his ancestors, some miles out of the town,or to meet the envoys of the Chinese Emprrior,a short way out of the west gate of the capital and at a place where a peculiar sort of triumphal arch, half built in masonry, and half in lacquered wood, has been erected close by an artificial cut in the rocky hill, which, in honour of the Chinese meaiengera, goes by the name of "Pekin Pass." In Corea all the towns are walled, everybody must be in by sunset, and nobody must go out before sunrise. So the rush of travellers and others just before sunset for the heavy gates is often amusing to heir upon. At night; the hoarse voice of the gatekeepers may be heard shouting out that time is up, and ,hurrying the weary traveller i to enter the precincts of the Royal city ; then the huge iron padlocks and bolts are fastened, the gate- keepers retire to the adjoining lICURO to continue the interrupted gambling which accupies their day, and a few rusty old sprars standing in a row on a rack are left to take care of the safety of the town and of its inhabit- ants. With the sun every noise ceases, every good citizen retires to his house, and only an occasional leopard now and then crawls over the city wall and makes pere- grinations in the darkness over the capital. Signal fires are a common expedient in the interior of Corea. The Coreans are extremely superstitious, as the writer dis- covered when he skeichA a small boy in a crowd. The mother thought the foreigner's work must bring a cala- mity upon her OM. "There was a piercing yell and the pale woman looked such daggers at me that I nearly dropped the sketch, brushes, and pallette out of my hands. Then, with another yell even more piercing than the first she made a dash into the crowd and tried to snatch the child away. However, she was not suc- cessful in her attempt, for my audience had got so in- terested in the picture that they would not hear of let- ting the child go; hut the unfortunate part of all this was that the angry mother was pulling the child by the head and one arm trying to drag him away, while the people on the other side were pulling him as hard as they could by the other arm and the legs, so that the poor screaming mite was nearly torn to pieces and no remonstrating on my part had any effect on this tug-of- war. Fortunately for the child, the mother let go; but it was certainly not fortunate for the others, for, follow- ing the little ways that women have, even in Corea, she proceeded to scratch the faces of all that were within reach, and I myself came within an inch of having my eyes scratched out of my head by this infuriated parent, when to my great relief they took her away. As she re- entered the door she shook her fist, and thrust out her torgue at me."—" Fortnightly Review."

div.head: A. LIVERPOOL II 0 RROR.
div.p: A. LIVERPOOL II 0 RROR.

Attention is called in the "Liverpool Daily Post" te what appears to he a disgraceful state of things at the " lairages " or receptacles for imported cattle at Wood- side, Liverpool. So great has been the increase in this trade on the Mersey that the Liverpool Dock Board re- ceives from this source alone about £70,000, yet no at- tempt has been made to keep pace with the demand for accommodation. When a cattle steamer comes along- side these lairages they are found to be already full, and some of them have to be hastily cleared to make room for the fresh arrivals. The cattle are driven, often at night time, into an old corn warehowe, into which they ascend by a gangway five feet wide, two hundred feet long, and with a dangerous incline. Bydint of beating, the unfortusaate beasts are driven up, and often they arrive seriously injured. The gored and maimed are then dragged out and sent down a shoot or lift, dead or dy- ing,for immediate slaughtering. When they come down again the animals frequently arrive in a confused mass, with broken legs and wrenched horns,frantic,and goring one another horribly. Serious accidents also happen to the men in charge of them. Apart from the torture in- flicted upon the poor beasts, there is the pecuniary loss on tileir value to he considered,so that it is not surpris- ing to find that importers are bestirring themselves to get a reform effected.

div.head: Sunlight
div.p: Sunlight
TUESDAY.

In the House of Commons on Tuesday, Mr. Asputru, in reply to a question relative to the recent attack on Irish haymaker; at Altcar and the sentences at Liverpool Assizea on the ringleaders,said English judges and juries were evidently quite prepared to enforce the law im- partially. Sir E. GREY stated that the Government had not yet received the decision of the Federal Judge at Salta in the case of Jabez Balfour. On the motion of Sir WILLIAM HARCOURT, it was re- solved, on a division, by a majority of 39, that the pro- ceedings on the Miners', Eight Hours Bill, if under dis- cussion at midnight, should not be interrupted. The House went into committee on the bill, resuming con- sideration of the amendment moved by Mr.D.A.Triorsas, that the Act should not be adopted in any county unless a majarity of the workmen employed were in favour of it. Mr. G. BALYOUR, continuing his speech, said the bill was really a step towards collectivism, that its ob- ject was to keep up the price of coal and the rate of wages. He moved an amendment setting forth that local option should be exercised in regard to the powers of the bill, not in counties, but in districts to be drawn up by the Hosix SECRETARY. This alteration was made in Mr. THOMAS'S amendment. After further discussion Mr. J.A. PEASE moved an amendment to the amendment that two-thirds of the miners in any district should decide whether they were in favour of local option or not. This amendment was ultimately withdrawn. Mr. J.CwasszEs- LAIN said it appeared to him there was not the slightest chance of the bill in its present form passing this session. Ifon the other hand, the promoters would allow the amendment to be passed without necessarily admitting the grounds for its acceptance they would secure a very useful hill and gain for everybody a vast amount of ex- perience. He appealed to those in charge of the Dill to make some concessions. At ten minutes to eight o'clock Mr. Fxsmicx rose to address the House, but on the mo- tion of Mr. WOODS the closure was carried by a majority of 22. 'Cho committee then divided on Mr. THOMAS'S amendment, and the figures were—For the amendment, 112; against, 107 ; majority for the amendment, 5. Amid a scene of excitement the Chairman, on the mo- tion of Mr. RORY, put the question that he report pro- gress, and the "Ayes "had it. The bill,it was intimated, would be withdrawn.

In the House of Lords on Tuesday evening Lord SALTS. BURY intimated • that in view of Sir W. HARCOURT'S declaration in the Rouse of Commons no good purpose I would he served by pressing on the Immigration of Aliens Bill. The debite on the motion for the second reading of the E?icted Tenants Bill was resumed by the Duke of DEVONSHIRE, who declared that there was no precedent for such a measure. It was a proposal to force back upon the owner of the soil tenants who had deliberately forfeited the protection conferred upon them by a long course of legislation. It was not an amnesty but a re- vival of war. The appflcation of the " gag " in the House of Commons had destroyed all chance of com- promise on the measure, and he found it impossible to vote for the bill. Lord ASIIBC)URNE having opposed the bill, the Lord CHANCELLOR r9marked that if the bill had been introduced by Lord SALISBURY it would have been adopted. The prearranged rejection of a measure which had been passed by a majority ot the House of Commons was a degradation of that House. The settlement of the question on the lines proposed by the bill would be a gain not only to the Government but to those who hoped to take their places. Lord HALSBURY (ex-Chancellor) op- posed the bill, and he was followed by Lord CLANRI- CARD; who gave some statistics with regard to the evic- tions and reinstatements on his own estates in Galway and elsewhere. Lord SALISBURY summed up the de- bate from the point of view of the Opposition. He denied that they were actuated simply by vindictive feelings against those who had broken the law. Lord ROSEBERY replied. He denied that the Gov-rnment had introduced the hill without due preparation, and said the measure was founded on the report of the Mathew Commission. He rebuked Lord CLANRICARDE and Lord SALISBURY for the jeering spirit in which they had referred to the suf- ferings of tenants. Referring to the prediction by the MARQUIS of SALISBURY that the fall of the House of Lords would involve that of the Rouse of Commons, he said he did not predict that their Lordships' House would be de- stroyed. But their power of veto was attacked, and there was much in the air that should make them walk warily. It was not possible for that House, since the franchise had been so largely extended, to claim equal power with the freely elected representatives of the people. The House divided, when there appeared for the second reading 30, against 249 ; and the bill was accord- ingly rejected.

WEDNESDAY. In the House of Commons on Wednesday the Miners' Eight Hours Bill was withdrawn. The debate on the.order for going into Committee on the Indian Budget was resumed. Mr. S. SMITH had moved for an inquiry into the finances of India and the condition of the people. Sir A. SCOBLII said the disloca- tion of the finances of India had arisen from the con- stant depreciation of the rupee. In deference to the demands of Lanea,hire—demands which had been listened to under stress of political considerations—no import duty had been allowed to be levied upon Lanca- shire piece goods, and he considered the refusals of the home Government to allow the Government of India to impose that tax was a very serious dereliction of duty towards the people of linina. Sir RICHARD TEMPLI held that the people of India were no poorer than the people of England. He congratulated the Government on hav- ing the courage and foresight to refuse to accede to the resolution of the House of rommotis on simultaneous examinations. What, he asked, would become of the public debt if the European army were sent home and 1 the European civil officers were dispensed with? Mr. 1 FowLiza,in reply,said lie intended to make his Indian Bud- get statement on Thursday. Their supreme consideration, ,he asserted, should be the benefit of the people of India. ' The mover and seconderofthresoliitiaflhai.maifltained that the financial administration of India w s defective, unjust, and extravagant. The true test was whether the government of India by England had been a failure or had promoted the prosperity of the people. He showed how in many ways it had had the latter effect. He said the Government were not prepared to refer the Constitution of India to a Select Committee, but if Mr. SMITH would withdraw his motion the Government at the beginning of next session would propose the appoint- ment of a Select Committee to inquire into the condition of the Indian revenue both in India and in England. Mr. SMITH withdrew his resolution. the House went into Committee, pro formd, on the Indian Budget, and pro- gress was reported. The Railway and Canal Traffic Bill was read a third time. _

div.head: AN IRON-FRAMED PIANIST.
div.p: AN IRON-FRAMED PIANIST.

Signor Gravagni, a Milanese pianist, made a bet that he would play for twenty-five consecutive hours, with only one interval of half-an-hour for refrestiment,and he won triumphantly, for he went straight on without even taking the stipulated period of rest. Starting at eleven at uight, he kept on until midnight on the following day, playing worki by Wagner, comic operas, ballet music, and grand opera. From time to time he was fed by a friend, who poured down his throat coffee, tea,and Marsala wine with beaten-up eggs. A jury of eight musicians took it in turns to watch the performance. So far from being exhausted at the end of these extra- ordinary proceedin,gs, Signor Gravagni offered to make a further bet of £4O that he would keep on for another six hours, but there we no takers.

div.head: BE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, AUGUST 18, 1894:
div.p: BE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, AUGUST 18, 1894:

IT may, we think, be safely pre- Evicted Tenants. Minerq And dieted that both the Bills which were defeated in Parliament on Tuesday will he heard of hgaia. There are few things more certain in the politics of t'ae day than that the Eight Hours Bill for miner 3 has only been deferred, not destroyed. Even in the present House of Commons there is a c'ear majority in favour of the principle of the Bill. The adverse vote of Tuesday was given on an amendmetit moved by Mr. D. THOMAS, a Welsh colliery pro- prietor, providing that an Eight Hours Act should only operate in districts in which a major- ity of miners voted in its favour. Thi s amend- ment, which was carried by a majority of fiveiwas considered by the proMoters of the Bill to be fatal '1 to the objects they have in view and rather than accept it they have withdrawn the measure for the present session. They have rejected a corn promise in the expectation that before long all their demands will be conceded. Nor is it likely that they will be disappointed. Conversion upon this eight-hours question has proceeded at a very rapid rate. At a meeting of the Miners' Federation on Wednesday it was declared that the Bill had been defeated by a "curious combination of coalowners on both sides of the Heuse, miners' agents of the two northern counties, the renegade Liberals, and the bulk of the Tory party." As a matter of fact the real core of the resistance is to be found in the fact that there iz still a considerable minority of the miners themselves in opposition to the Bill. Once let this minority, or the bulk of it, he converted to the policy of the Miners' Federation and the Bill is as good as passed. There are already many indications that the minority will soon fall into line with the Federation miners. The representatives in Par- liament of the pitmen of Durham and Northurn- ber;and wore on Tuesday as strong as ever in their opposition, but the ground is crumbling away beneath them. Their constituents are beginning to view the Bill wig' increasing favour, and ilo is probable that before another twelve months have passed over there will be a distinct majority in its favour even in the two northern counties.

The treatment which the Evicted Tenants Bill received in the House of Lords was something like that accorded to the Home Rub.: Bill ; that is to say, it was intemperately denounced and finally thrown out hv an overwhelming majority- -249 to 30. Of this Bill, or of a Bill with a similar object in view, there is bound to he something more heard. The social wound which it was meant to cure will remain for a few months longer, but it cannot be allowed to remain for ever. Four- fifths of the Irish people demand that a remedy shall be applied, and that demand is backed up by the whole of the Liberal party. The landlords who control the House of Lords, may With that unwisdom which they have often displayed in con- nection with the Irish affairs, delay the hand of the reformer for a time,but in the end they will be foictsd to 10.41/41 Abide.

THERE have been thirty-three The Irish thousand three hundred and Tragedy. seventy-five evictions in Ireland since 1881. This is the information which Mr. Joni* MORLEY, the Chief Secretary for Ireland gave the House of Commons on Thursday after- noon. Is it to be wondered :it that there is still a land question in Ireland ? In every one of these cases the ejected tenant has lost all claim to his property in the holding, which, it is said, was 'n many instances more valuable than that of On landlord himself. Mr. CHAMBERLAIN atked what had become of all these evicted families, but that was a question which Mr. MORLEY could not answer. It may be inferred that a certain propor- tion of them have been reinstated as mere care- takers uf the land which had been improved or reclaimed by their own labour or that of their progenitors. If the fortunes of the others were disclosed there can be no doubt that some painful chapters would be added to the tragic history of the Irish peasantry. Banished as they have been from the land out of which they had hitherto drawn' a subsistence,however scanty,they will in number.- less instances have had no choice but to swell the ranks of the unemployed in the large towns of England and America. In this way the circle of suffering which is begun in Ireland is extended to every cf4mninnity amongst whom the expatriated tenants take refuge. In the meantime the littlø. farms which are now tenantless are returning tcr the state of wilderness and bog from which Oil. were originally reclaimed. At the same time that the land laws of Irelmd still leave so much to be desired from the point of view of the tenant the landlords are not faring badly. On the same afternoon that he gave .fte information with re' gard to the number of evictions,Mr. Morley stated that the su m which had been paid to Irish laud' lords through the landed estate courts and the encumbered estates court amounted to no less & figure than fifty-six millions of pound,;. Tenants - evicted by thousands, landlords remuner- ated with , millions ! Such is the working of even the reformed and system of Ireland, end some people affect to be surprised that Irishmen do not rest content beneath it.

to a serious extent, , but, at the same time they have caused a great demand for labour. The most improved of reaping machines are of little use when ths corn has" lost its legs " and the scyther or even the still more old-fashioned sickle, has t° be brought into use. T.te result is that in the current number of the " LAhour Gazette" the only class of labourers who are returned as" well employed" are those eogaged in agriculture. -15 far as other classes f workmen .are concerned the reports are not satisfactory. The fifty-two trade' unions, with an aggregate membership of 358,5d5r make returns to the Labour Department to the effect that they had 26,576 of their members linear • ployed at the end of July, or 7.4 per cent., as core" pared with 6.3 per cent. in June and 6.2 per cent for July 1893. The decrease of employment mgr however, to some extent be accounted for by the Scottish miners' strike and the strike of moulders' and patternmakers on the North-eat coast, us both of these strikeg indirectly affect a large nwP" ber of people who have nothing to do with the matters in dispute.

EXCURSION FROM RUNCORN TO CHESTER. I On Wednesday morning shortly after nine o'clock, tee choristers of Holy Trinity Church, Runcorn. accompanied by a number of the congregation, with the Rev. Dr. Preston, vicar ; the Rev. A. Bertram, Messrs.Hankinson, Lea and J. Horsefield stetted from Runcorn station on a trip to Chester. On their arrival at the ancient city they spent their time in a variety of pleasant ways, sub- sequently adjou ruing to Norbury's refreshment rooms for tea They afterwards indulged in a sail on the Dee as far as Eaton Hall, some of the members betaking themselves to the woods. The weather during the day was somewhat showery but not sufficiently S 9 to mar the pleasure sought by the choristers and their friends. The return home was very enjoyable, and altogether the outing was a p ronounced success. OUTING OF RUNCORN CHORISTERS TO SOUTHPORT. The members of the Primitive MethodisXhapel Choir, Greenway-road, Runcorn, had their annual trip on Mon- day last when they travelled by train from Widees station to Southport. Among the party was Mr. W. Gittens junr., the choir master. They arrived at Seuth- poet shortly after 12 o'clock, and immediately made their way to Churclidown Gardens where for some tine they enjoyed an inspection of the flowers and shrubbery. The weather was beautiful. Tea was subsequently partaken of in the gardens after which they returned to Southpore and visited many places generally known to possess in- teresting features. At length a move was made towards the railway station where they boarded the 8.5 train for Widnes. -After a pleasant ride they reached this town and afterwards proceeded to Runcorn, everyone being of the opinion that the excursion had been one of the most enjoyable ever experienced. LECTURE ON "PARISH COUNCILS" AT RUNCORN. On Thursday night a lecture on tl:e above subject was delivered by the Rev. James Hanby, of Halton. under the auspices of the Runcorn and Vicinity United crades and Labour Council in the Trades Hall, St. John-street, Runcoro. Mr. A. R. Norman occupied the chair and there was a fairly large gathering. After a few int;o- ductory remarks by the Chairman, the Rrv. J. Hanby proceeded with his lecture, the subject of which he said had, with the greatest difficulty, been placed upon the statute hook by the present administration with Mr W. E. Gladstone at its head. fie then went on to exVaiti the working of the measure and how it would effect the various districts. His observations were listened to with the greatest attention,and at the close of the proceedings a hearty vote of thanks was accorded him. SOARING RAIN PROOF. OVERCOATS, yet porous. Esr., C. div.head: RETURN OF THE RUNCORN VOLUNTEERS FROM
div.p: RETURN OF THE RUNCORN VOLUNTEERS FROM

BLACKPOOL. The men composing the F and GCompanies of the 2nd (Earl of Chester's) V.B.C.R.,returned on Saturday even- ing to Runcorn from their week's encampment at Black- pool, with the remainder of the regiment. They all looked s miewhat tanned in consequence of their soi)uro at this resort, and were apparently improved in health. At the inspection on the previous day the men were compliment:A by the inspecting officer, Colonel W. V. Browntow,whp said that there had been a marked mi provement,some of them being very smart indeed. The march past was very good, as also had been the manual and firing exvrcises. He expressed the pleasure which he would this year experience in giving them a vtry favourable report all rounchand especially more so would tills be the case seeing that it would be the last time he would havean opportunity of inspecting them. Remark, of 4 similar nature were also passtd concerning them by Brigadier-General Carey, while he was awarding sev.ral prizes which had been secured in various competitions subsequent to the inspection. On the following Saturday morning,before leaving the encampment for tile railway station, Colonel Ashton spoke to the battalion in eulo- gistic terms upon their turnout and efficient drill. Tho Runcorn section arrived at their headquarters in Green- way-road shortly before eight o'clock in the evening, the delay being caused at South Shore, where the men were kept waiting for nearly two hours for their train. SEWING MACHINES. Hand £2 184. Gil. Trc, die £4 tk.wil handsom, vnlnut cover.—J and W. Durros, 15 and 18, Sankey-st., Warrington.—Advt. ACCIDENT TO JUDGE WYNNE-FFOULKES. An alarming accident befel Judge Wynne- Ffoulkes while driving in a cab from Winsiord County Court to the station on Wednesday. . The horse, which was frightened by a truction engine. bolted and came down as the driver attempted to turn a sharp corner. Tile vehicle was smashed, kr the judge, fortunately, escaped unscathed, though considerably shaken. His usher, who was riding on the b-,x, was thrown violently into the street, one of the wheels passing over him. On being medically examined, he was found to be suffering from a severe fracture of one of his legs above the ankle. He was subsequently removed to bias home at Birkenhead in charge of two ambulance men. His Honour Judge Wynne-Ffoulkes was able to follow his duties at the Warrington County Court an Thursday. CROQUET.—GARLAND, 51, Bridge-street, Warrington. Advt.

REGISTRATION OF PLUMBBIIS. At a meeting of the Registration CommiVee of the District Gouncil for West LfitlcaAire, Cheshire, and Nort h Wales, held at the secretary's office, 28 Church-street, Liverpool, Dr. Vacher, presiding, 22 applications from plumbers (10 masters, 12 opera- Lives) for their names to be placed on the national reuister were laid before the committee by the secretary, Mr. William Unsworth. The qualifioations of each applicant were carefully considered, with the result that six masters and seven operatives were approved to be recommended to the Worship- ful Company of Plumbers, London, to be registfrecl. Throe masters and two operatives were postponed • for the applicants to produce further documentary .evidence with proof of their training, practical experience, and skill in the work of a ?lumber. Two operatives. were requested to submit to an examination into the principles and practice of the trade, and two were referred to the Pre-ton Local Committee to be inquired into locally. The resigna- tions of Mesq.e. Ewing and Thomas as members of the committee were received and accepted with regret, and Messrs. W. H. Coward and R. R. Ellis were unanimously elected master representatives to fill the vacancies. Letters from six members of Parlitiment were read as to their supporting the Piumbers' Reuistration Bill, 1894. WESLEYAN METHODIST LOCAL PREACHERS' MUTUAL AID ASSOCIATION.

On Sunday,sermons were preachud in aid of this association in the chapels in Altrincham Wesleyan Circuit. Mr. Moses Atkinson, of Leeds, and Mr. S. Rathbone Edge, M.A., J.P., of Newcastle-under- Lyme, preached at Bank-street Chapel, Altrincham, and Biwdon Chapel alternately. The Timperley pulpit was occupied by Mr. Cunliffe, of Oldham, and Mr. Surnmersgill, of Sankey Bridges, Warring- ton. Mr. Ea !son, of the Manchester Prison Gate Mission, conducted the services at the Borough- road Mission, Altrincham, and als ) addressed the men of Mr. William ChampneWs Bible Class at the Bank-street Lecture Hall in the afternoon. Mr. Cranshaw, of Manchester, discoursed at the Booth Bank Chapel anti at Hale-road Chapel, Altrincham, and Vicarage-lane Clive), Bowdon, Messrs. Bescohy and Summersgill pr..qached. •Mr. Gawkrodger was the preacher at the Broadheath Mission. The col- lections at the various places of worship amounted to about £35. The objects of the association in aid of which these sermons were preached on Sunday are to afflrd relief to its members during periods of sickness and in old age, and also to provide a sum of money for their decent interment. It appears that it was formed at the latter end of the year 1849, and now numbers 7,352 members, of these 2 024 are honorary members, receiving no relief ; from the funds.

LOCAL SUCCESSES AT BLACKPOOL SHOW. Among the prize winners at the Blackpool Agri- cultural Show is Sir Gilbert Greenall, who has car- ried off the second prize for gelding or rare for hackney purposes, second for pony, first for gelding or mare with trap and harness (15 hands high and upwards), and second for the same under 15 hands.

LOCAL INTER-CLUB CYCLE RACE. On Saturday, the Makertield Cycling Club and Golborne Cycling Club held an inter .club 50 miles handicap, team race, and championship. The prizes were : handicap, Ist, gold medal ; 2nd, gold centred medal; 3rd, silver medal. Team race, winning team to receive gold centred medals at the expense of the losing team. Championships gold medal. The six fastest time men in each club to count in the team race, and the competitor doing the distance in the shortest time to take the championship gold medal, kindly presented by Mr. T. Cooper, Market- street, Earlestown. The course selected was the Anfield 50 miles, and although the roads were thick with mud, and rain still falling, a start was made at 4.39 p.m., the Golborne team refiring to have.t he race postponed. The scratch man (T. Garton) was started at four minutes past five, and passed Cooper with three minutes start at four miles out, at half , distance he had passed all the other competitors, ' and came in an easy winner by 16 minutes, despite his fall when nearly half distance had been covered, : thus winning the handicap and championship gold medals, and also gold centred medal in the team race. Ile was well paced throughout by Mr. C. Lucas, of Liverpool, and Messrs. 11 . Turner and S. Heywood, of Manchester. W. Raynoi who recently won the Makerfield 10 miles handicap, got 2ad place. A. J. Millard, who secured second place in the 10 miles mentioned above, was the 3rd man to finish, and was closely followed by Hardy, Parting- ton and Wright, in the order named. Thus the Makertield team finished the first six men, whereas the Golborne team tailed to get a single man placed. Although defeated by such long odds, the oolhorne nitm are not yet sati,fidd, but have again challenged Makerfleld to run over ~he same course, for gold centred inenals, with four men from each club, providing that Alakerfield dots not run the scratch man (Garton). This has been accepted.

div.head: THINGS HEARD AND SEEN AT
div.p: THINGS HEARD AND SEEN AT
RUNCORN. BY AN OCCASIONAL CONTRIBUTOR.

Once more we are resting peacefully in our beds with•a sense of security. But why ? Vbat : don't you know? Our volunteers have come back from their encampment at Blackpool; each of them I near a few inches taller. You don't know the cause, well tell you. Colonel Brownlow who you know very well, doesn't blarney too much, told them ever so many good things after the inspection. They had made a marked improvement in their appearance, and were very smart indeed. The march past was good,as well as the manual and firing exercises.; and he was pleased at having an opportunity, on this, the last time he would inspect them, of giving them a very favourable report. 1 heard that some of our Runcornians carried off przes on the Friday afternoon too for the neute,t rigged tent and the neatest row of tents. In fact it was a case of" See the conquering hero(es)c?-mes” when they were marching from Runcorn btfitiOn in the evening after being kept waiting on South Shore railway, station for two hours. Runcorn is surely rich in musical talent, and the possessors of this tale.nt must also be credited with a large amount of determination. One sect bit of the body to whom 1 now allude is obviously tlie Runcorn Musical Society, the members of which held their annual meeting a few nights ago. The secretaries' report was very satisfactory, nut of course left room for an iMproveMent. Where is the society that cannot be improved? The Buccesstul efforts of this muAcal combination to present such a favourable state of things, more especially as regards finances, are really deserving of sincere Praise, I don't think it has been a very easy work, but the workers have been determiiled and energetic, and are fast nearing their coveted goal. With a little outside assis:ance they will reach it sooner, and such aid can be warmly reccm- mended.

The residents of Weston Point have scored one ; that is to say, if the County Council places implicit reliance in its committee, who have just finished their inquiry into the subject of dividing the town- ship into wards. The claim was manifestly a very fair one, and this the committee fortunately recog- nised ; and before leaving, they stated that it was their intention to make u recommendation to the Council to Issue an order dividing the township intl.) wards._ The result has given the most lively satisfaction to those residing at Weston Point, and this place will accordingly have the power, under the Local Government Act, 1894, 01 sending five parish councillors to represent them at the delibera- tions of the Council. The township will also have one district councillor and one guardian.

div.head: WIDNES CYCLE CLUB.
div.p: WIDNES CYCLE CLUB.

On Thursday evening the annual championship sports, under the auspices of the Widnes Cycle Club, were held on the enclosure of the Old Boys' Football Club, Wavertree. There was only a small attend- ance. It is unfortunate that there is not a suitable racing track near Widnes, as both the attendance and entries suffered in consequence of the distance. The fo:- lowing were the officials: —Judge, Mr. J. Timmins ; starter, Mr. J. Hearne; timekeeper, Mr. W. Cook ; secretary, Mr. C. Bridgstock ; treasurer, Mr. S. Beesley ; committee, Messrs. T. H. Thomas, J. Timmins, W. Tay- lor, and S. Beesley. Results : Five Miles Championship.-1, D. Daigleish ; 2, F. Sherratt ; 3, W. Sherratt. Only four members turmo out for this event, W. Jackson being the other rider. Dalgleish made the pace from the start, followed by F. Sherratr, W. Sherratt and Jackson in the order named. The riders maintained their positions until the seven- teenth lap, when Jackson forged ahead of the brothers Stierratt, and upon entering the eighteenth lap DaWeish and Jaekson were abreast. During the last lap Vie brothers Sherratt regained their position at the expense of Jaekssn, who fell upon entering tht straight. Dalele- ish won by a yard, three yards separated second and third. Time. 15 mins. 54 4.5 secs. One I‘Re Novices flandicap.-1, A. Ward, 50 :ards ; 2, W. Taylor, scratch ;3, A. Webstn, 80. Won by ten yard, twenty yards between second and third. Two Miles Handicap.-1, F. Sue.rratt. 170 yanis ; 2, W. Jackson, 120 yards; 3, F. Franklin, 210. Five started for this event, which resuted in an exciting race between Sherratt and Jackson. The former, however. 11 gained a big lead in the last lap, and won by tzn yards ; la bad third. Time, 5 mina. 43 secs.

div.head: FOOLISH BRIDEGROOM AT
div.p: A FOOLISH BRIDEGROOM AT
ST. 11 ELENS.
ROBBED OF 430.

A young couple who were on Wednesday married at one of the Nonconformist Churches in S. Helens havc, it is said, had a most unpleasant experience. As the days of courting were iirar the termination, a house was taken in the distrier of Denton's-green,and the furnishers began to deliver their goods. The bridegroom was so satisfied with the security of his new home that before taking personal possession he deposited a sum of be- tween £l3O and £l4O in a secretaire, and locked up the house. Sone evit-disposed per6on or persons had evi- dently watched the manwavres, and were bent on se- curing some of the goods for themselves. An entrance was effected a few nights ago, and when the house was visited again by the lawful occupants they found that the secretaire had been broken open and the whole of the money taken. Some of the other valuables and goods had been tied up ready for taking away, tut when the thief or thieves made such a. " find " they left the other az ticles, and were content with the ready cash. The police were inti4rmed of the occurrenc,., but up to Wedne•iday night nothing has been traced. The couple were married as stated, but their loss on the eve of their wedding had the effect .1 casting a gloom over tie nappy proceedings.

div.head: NEWTON COMMISSIuNERS.
div.p: NEWTON COMMISSIuNERS.

A meeting of this body was held in the Town Hall Earlestown, on Monday. Mr. J. W. Emmett occu- pied the chair and there were also present. Messrs. W. Collingwood, T. Ormand, G. Ratcliffe, P. McMahon, E. T. Evans, P. Thompson, J. Smith, J. E. Worsley (law clerk) and R. Brierley (clerk and surveyor.)

div.head: GAS AND WATER COMMITTEE.
div.p: GAS AND WATER COMMITTEE.

At a meetin;;oi this committee held on July 16th the gas manager's report was read and on his verb4l com- munications to the meeting i was resolved to postpone consideration of regemerator furnaces to next summer or spring. The earbon;zing account for the past mouth was read giving fuel used 153 tons 12 c wts, gas made 1,516, 500 it. -being an average of 10.069 ft. per ton of fuel used. The minutes were passed.

HIGHWAYS COMMITTEE. Meeting held Monday July 16th. Dr. Watkins, medical officer of health attended to submit and read his quar- terly report which summarised gives, births 129, deaths 36, excess of births 93. The births were equal to 373 per 1,000 of the estimated population, and the deaths 105 per 1000. Sixteen eases of infectious diseases were reported during the quarter. A letter Was read from the Local Government Board on the subject of Newton mere and brook, when it was resolved that a copy of the letter be furnished to the Medical Officer of Health. The , quotations of the Dee Clwyd Granite Company for the supply of broken stone for road purposes for the ensu- ing year were accepted. Mr. Thomas Scott having com- plained that toll had been demanded from his tenant in respect of the strip af land in front of Mr. Scott's pre- mises next to the police station in Market-street, it was resolved that the Law Clerk inform Mr. Scott that upon his leaving the land.unenclosed, toll would not be de- manded in respect of it. Mr. Gregory's report was read and approved. Plans for 12 cottages on Newton Com- mon for Mr. W. Waterworth were submitted and deterred on the question of drainage and common rights. The minutes ware passed.
FINANCE COMMITTEE. , At a meeting of the above cotninittee held on Monday July l6h, accounts amounting to £657 13s. 11d, were passed for payment. The minutes were passed.
_ THE MEDICAL OFFICER. On the proposition of Mr. Emmett, seconded by Mr. E. T. Evan, Dr. Watkins was re-appointed medical officer of health.
THE POSTAL ARRANGEMENTS.-DEPUTATION
FROM NEW fON.

The Chairman s7ailii;h-a(7l- no doubt that most or the members of that board had seen the letters which had :fripeared in the local newspapers during the last few weeks, written by Weir friends at Newton, complaining loudly of the Commissioners. because they were trying to get better postal facilities for Eat lestown. They would remember that this postal business was left in the hands of a sub-committee to arrange with the post office olti- cials for better postal facilities for that end of the town- I ship. The committee had had One or two interviews with Mr. Rieh and he stated to them, that what Earles- town wanted could not he given until a better post office was provided, and it was for Earlestown to provide a suitable huilding. A plan of the proposed building had been submitted to that gentleman and he had returned it, suggesting certain alterations. That was how the matter stood. He (the chairman) was very sorry to say that Mr. Brierley had committed a breach of confidence with the committee. A person from Newton catne to Mr. Brierley and put some questions to him,asking what. the committee was; doing t f provide a post office, and he told him all that the committee hail done, and also allowed him to examine the deeds, conferring the land on which the Public Hall stood, to the Commissioners. They might judge of his (Mr. Emmett's) surprise when he saw part of the committee's proceedings in the local newspapers, two days afterwards, seeing that the sub- comeaittee were net in a position to report fully to the Board as to the arrangements come to with the Port Office authorities. He would leave the Boars' to ferm their own opinion of Mr. Brierley's action. The com- mittee was trying to make the best postal arrangements it could, and hoped before long to be able, to report it to the Board. He thou,,ht, it was his duty to maka those remarks seeing that they were going to have a deputa- tion from Newton on the matter. Mr. Smith said he thought it ought to he made known that the-sub-committee endeavoured not only to get. better facffities for Earlestown, but also for Newton. He thought the remarks that were made in the public newspapers, re'ative to the deputation of the Comtnis- sinners to Mr. Rich, were very ungenerous. The deputa- tion did all they could for Earleatown and also for Newton at the same time. They did not go pledged for better postal accommodation for Eirlestown, alone, hut they obtained better postal facilities for Newton. It was very ungenerous of anybody to write to the newspapers say- ing that the matter was one-sided. Mr. Riteliffe said he thought the committee was keep- ing something back from the Board, when they got all , information as to what was being done by the commit- tee, from the Newton end of the township. ' Mr. Ormand said it would appear from the letters in the newspapers that the committee had acted one-sided, and altogether unfair to Newton. Asa member of that : sub-committee he must say that that was incorrect. They had not stood to better themselves at the expense of Newton. According to the newspapers the N wtoti 0,-ople had been trying to better themselves at Earles- tow n's expense. , Mr. McMahon said the Newton people seemed to know the committee's business better than they did them- selves. _ _ _

Mr. Brierley read a letter from the Local Government Board in which it stated that Mr. Barton, chairman of the Newton Ratepayer's Committee, had-written, asking whether the Newton Board of Commissioners were empowered to spend public money in the erection of a psst office at Eirlestown The Local Government Beard agsed to be supplied with the deliberations of the Com- missioners on the matter.—On the motion of the Chair- man, seconded by Mr. Ratcliffe, the letter was referred to the sub-committee. After the Boar i had proceeded with some business in committee, the depteation from Newton entered. Tne following comprised the deputation : Messrs. F. Wood, R. Barton, Simpson, Adams and Syme. Mr. Wood said they waited upon the Commis- sioners by appointment as a deputation from the Wards Committee of the Newton Ratepayers Association to discuss the past office airangements for the district. They admitted at once that ilia p )St office accommodation at Earlestown was not what was necessary, but at the same time they were in the same position. at Newton. They were aware that tlie Com- missioners had submitted plans to the postal aotaorities, and from an inspection of those plans they were quite 'agreed that a building erected on land adjoining the Town H ill could not he put up without considerable expense, and it was the eXpense they to: k objection to. It was usual for post offices • to be erected by private enterprise, as was the. ease at Widnes and other places, and not out of the rates. If the Commissioners had power to erect a post offie ad- joining that hall, there was still the question whether the laud was given for that purpose. As that Beard would in a few weeks go out of office, and ad !Rion& members were to ha elected, they considerei that the question of providing a post office for Earlestown was ono that might very well stand over until that time, in order to give the ratepayers an opportunity to expres. their opinion by their votes at the forthcoming election. The Chairman said the complaint of the deputation seemed to he that the Commissioners were seeking to erect a post office out of the rates.—Mr. Wood : Not al- together.—Mr. Emmett continuing said that N icton did not say one word about postal arrangements until after the Commissioners had taken the matter up with the postal authorities. If they were going to take something from Newton in any shape or form he could understand them coming there that day. He (the Chairman) could not at present tell them where the money for the pro- posed post office was coming from until the arrange- ments were completed with the postal authorities. Mr. Simpson considered that the Newton people were quite justified in seeing the Commissioners when they bound that they had already submitted a plan of a build• ing which would cost £2,000. They Wanted to know whether they were going to do anything for Newton. The Chairman said Newton was throwing great obstacles in the way of Earlestown getting better postal facilities. A deputation from Newton had been to Mr. Rich, and told him what they were not warranted in saying, they had also written to the Local Government Board, and they now came to the Commissioners as a last resource. He thought the better, and more gentle- manly way for them to have followed, was to have ap- proached the Comnsissioners first.---Mr. Syme : The scheme was far advanced before we heard of it.—The Chairman : You hays been writing letters to the news- papers almost since the commencement.—Mr. Wood : We deny that in tnto —The Chairman : Well, one of the members who was to have formed the deputation had the courage to sign his name. Mr. Barton said that they at. Newton distinctly under- stood from certain authorities that the Commissinners were trying to get the head post offioe removed to Earlestown. Newton did not take any action until they saw in a local newspaper that the Commissioners were Preparing plans. They also found that it was prapossd to build on apiece of ground which the Commissioners had no right to use for that purpose. They had also no right t ) build it with public money. The .Nea ton rate- payers thought that the present Board—which was a stems gap Board—should not enter upon any big scheme until after the next election. There were also the ques- tions of night-soil and water, and these questions should be dealt with by the increased Beare. The Chairman said lie did not see why Earlestown should wait any longer for better postal facilities. They had waited long ere-sigh.

Mr. Adams said they had come to ask that the matter might to adjnurned until next November. Allowing that the ten present representatives would be re-elected there would he at, leabt five additional members who would make a worrierful difference in the composition ot the Board. There was only one representative. of Newton on that Board. Ile was surprised to hear from the Chairmin that he did not know where the money was coming frim. %Viten a plan was submitt,d it was generally understood how the building would be paid for. He obj,?cted to it, if it was to be paid out of the rates of the township.

Mr. Ormand said he gave a most emphatic denial to the charge that they at Earlestnwn were trying to re- move the head post office from Newton. All they were trying to do was to improve their postal arraegements— not at the expense ot Newton. The Newton arrange- ments were infinitely better than at Earlestown. He did not think it was very complimentary for the deputa- Oen !e call them a" stopgap "Board. Mr. Smith said he should like to endorse every word which had been said by Mr. Ormand, He would tell the deputation that they had ten representatives en that Board.. Anything they required for Newton would have the same careful attention as any other part of the township. It was a downright insult for them to say that they had only one representative on that Board. He (the speaker) represented Newton as much as any other part of the township.—Mr. Adams : Who elected you ?—Mr. Smith: You need not ask me that question. You know who elected me, and you are at liberty to take my place. The deputation to Mr. Rich from that Board got an extension of time for Newton as well as Earler,town.—Mr. Barton :—We had the extension of time before you went to Liverpool.— Mr. Smith : I say distinctly not. We were the means of getting that extension. Mr. Wood asked the Chairman whether he vvculd answer two questions for them. First : Whether the money for the new post office was to come out of the rates, and whether the question might be adjourned until after the November election.

The Chairman said he was finable at present to answer the first question. Tliy might borrow the moley from the Local Government 3oard, but they would not lend it to them until a proper inquiry had been held, and Newton _wouA have an opportunity of objecting to it.
!. Mr. Wood said his feeling in the mitr was that a post office should be built beiween EArlestown and Newt,m.
. _ Mr. Smith mid he thought if the Commi3sioners built two post offi,es, one at Earlestown and another at New- ton out of the rates, both wool" be satisfied.

Mr. Wood said it would be a waste of money to pro- vide two places. Mr. Smith wi,hed to know of a suitable placP. HP had heard two mentioned,Crow-lane,and the Mesnes,but he was of opinion that neither of them was suitable for the purpo!=e. Earlestown was not extending in the direction of Nev‘toa.

Several members of the deputation were of the opinion that the Meshes was a suitable place. The Chairman said it V7At, one of the most rediculous ideas he had heard of. The Newton depntation tried to impress Mr. Rich with that notion.—Mr. Barton denied that they did so.—The Chairman : It was reported that you did.—With re.lard to the question of deferring the matter until aft, r _November he (Mr. Emmett) would have to consult the Board.

-Mr. Wood asked that a reply be sent bv post to the secretary of the Newton Ratr-payers Commit t‘e. The Chairman promised that this should be done and the deputAtion w:tltdrow. . The 13.ard then resolved itself into committee to con- sider the matter.

div.head: TUE BOARD'S DECISION.
div.p: TUE BOARD'S DECISION.

Thr.. Secretary of the Newton Ratept7Qrs Committee has, we are informed, received a communication from Mr. Worsley. law clerk, to tbe Newton Commisioners, to the effect thlt the Commissioners will not proceed with the building of tho new post uffice at Earl,stown
until .the new board has hen ciccted in November next. This concession has been made in responseto the deputa- tion that waited upon the Commissioners on Monday. NEWTON RATEPAYERS COMMITTEE AND THE
ST. HELENS LICENSING SESSIONS
TEMPORARY AUTHORITIES NOT BINDING ON THE JUSTICES. _

A special sessions for the transfeeof public-house licences was held at St. Helens on Monday, the magis- trates on the bench being the Mayor (Aldermal Sinclair) in the chair, Aldermen T. Cooke and D. Wilechnie ; Councillors F. R. Dix,.n-Nuttall and H. Martin; Dr. Gask,ll. Messrs. W.G.iinble, C.C., J.Cotton, C. Sharpies, and B. A. Dromgoole.

The inagistra.les considered the licensed victuallers' applications first. The Maywr said the bench wished it to he Oistinctly understood that they did net consider the granting of a temporary authority at all tied the hands of the bench. An applicant must not expect to be licensed if he said he had paid any money to a previous tenant in the certainty that because he had got a tem- porary authority, he would get the licence. The magis- trates did not want that to be forgotten. Mr. Swift applied on behalf or Francis Cunningham for an extension of the temporary authority granted to him in respect of the Scar Inn, Merton-bank.

The Mayor said that, while granting the present appli- cation, they considered there had been plenty of room for improvement in the management of that house. The beersellers' applications were then considered and granted.

div.p: GOOD TENIPL.%_RS' CoNVESTION. HALF-YEARLY MEETING.

The half-yenrly session of No. 1 Convention of Good Templars in the S.W. Lancashire District was held on Saturday in the United M-thorlist Free Church Schools. St. Helen., whAi there was a good attendance of lodge dimities and repres-ntatives from lodges in Warrington, Wi,anes, Present, St.fielens, Earlestown, Leigh, and Tyldeslee. The session opened at 3.30, Bro. George Clarke, C.O T., of Earlestown, pre- siding. The usual press and credential cc minittees were appointed and the reports of various offi..!ers were tlin received. Bro. Clarke, C.C.T., referred to successful open air missions held at Present and St. Helens, and urged other lodges to engage in similar work,which was a splendid means of strengthening the membership and building up the lodge. He was pleased to report arrange ments for opening a new lodge in the Vulcan on the Thursday following,w;th very good prospects of a success.. ful future. In concluding, lie st Wed the Convention had just passed through its sixth anniversary, during Mild) it had been a very active body,and had Clone a good and useful work in helping on the lodges and spreading the principles of Good Temp'ary, and he hoped it would be even more succ,ssful iii the future.—Bro. E. Newman, C. Sec. ,stated that three new lodges had been instituted since February, the total membership in the area heir), 408,an increase nf 38 on the half-year. The attendance at in )ntltiy sessions had averaged 36, and the officers' attendance was also very good. Bro.Merris, , r.ty,rted on the Juvenile temples, several of which were doing well. and holding sirccessful meetings. A new temp'e had been opcnei at Tyliesley, Bro. J. Lindon C.E.S. referred to electoral matters show- ing that this :tweet of the tetnoerance question had received considerab'e attention during his term of office. The fiaancial report was read by Bro. George Tomlin, C. Trea.,.showing a balance in hand after clearing liabi- lities. Interesting reports of ledges and temples were neat given by reoresentatives present. The officers for the ensuing half-year were theta elected as follows : c.c.r., Bro. W. H. Dale, Earlestown; C. Co., Bro. Qi trtermaster-Sergeant Roberts, Warringt c.s.J.T., Bra. George E. Warbuttan, Earlestown ; Bro. John Taylor, E trlestawn ; C.V.T., Sister Mrs. Warbur- ton, Earlestown; C. Sec., Bro. E. Newman, Earlestown C. Trea., Bro. G-orge Tomlin, Warrington; C. Chap., Bro. J. Lindon, Present; C. Mar., Bro. J. T. Holliday, Earlestown; P.C.C. P., Bro. George Clarke, Earlestown ; C.D.M., Sister Mrs. Nurse, Warrington; (lA. Sec., Bro. Ashley, St. Helens; C.G., Bro. Williams, Bedford Leigh ; C. Sent., Bro. J. Blackmore, Widnes. It was decided to hold the next monthly meeting at Earlestown, on Satur- day, September Bth. Thanks were tendered to the re- tiring officers, and to the St. Helens friends for their arratnretnents for the session, which was then brought to a close,it having been of an interesting and encourag- ing character. A public tea was afterwards partaken of by a large number of members and friends.

John O'llrien was charged at the Warrington Petty Sessions 011 Wednesday, with having assaulted and othei wise ill-treated his wife Mary O'Brien on the ltitth June. The defendant did not appear, but a letter which had been sent to Sergeant Devlin was read, in which he said that he was going to have no more to do with the law the letter W:l9 also in defence of his conduct. Mr. A.. Browne, the solicitor for the complainant, stited that the defendant had, often, during th,- last two months, turned his wife out into the street at midnight with no other covering than her nightdress. He ha i also tried to strangl- her. Oa the 16th at June he struck her with a quart jug and turned her out of the house. On another occasion he threw a two pound tin of pepper over her head and face caw,i" her great pain. The defendant had been brought up for the same offence several times and in tive cases Mrs. O'Brien had begged him off, but his treatment had been 1 worse every time. Mr. Browne asked that the defend- ant might he committed to gaol and a separation order granted.—Mrs. O'Brien said that she was the wife of the I defendant and resided in Howard-street, Great Sankey. IShe bore out her solicitor's statement and witted for a separation order as she Was afraid to live with the defend- ant,her life being in danger. The last time he assaulted her she was in bed and under the treatment of Dr. Naden for eight days.—Mrs. Hughes, a witness, stated that she resided at 37, Howard-street, Great Sank,y, and on the 15th June last she took Mrs. O'Brien into her house at ene o'clock in the morning as the defendant had turnrd her out. Mrs. Hughes, said that she had done this 20 tor 30 times during the last two months. Last Monday Ishe heard Mrs. O'Brien Oicieking and on nnin7 t pe wnat was the matter,she foun•l the compl inant e.overed with pepper,tier eves and wraith being fill of it. Witness undressed her and put her to bed. On the 24th of July witness saw defendant trying to strang!e the complain- . ant.—Rebecca Woothanoti,er resident it. Howard-st.,also gave corr.orative eviJerme. The deft ndant's daughter I had been living with her some timets she was afraid of Ihis violene.. Howard-street was continually in an uproar through the defendant's cruelty to his_wife, and several neighbours h exprep•se a determination t I leave, if it was not stopped.—The magistrates sentence O'Brien to three months imprison- cut with hard laboir. and granted a s-paration order, °welling the defendant t tiC py 154. pr week towards : is wife's maintenance.

ACTION TO RECOVER RENT AT RUNCORN.

On Tuesday afternoon at the Runcorn County Clurt, before his honour Judge Wynne Ffoulkes William Wat kin, engineer, carrying on business as such tt Halton, sued George Fellows, of the same locality, for the sum of £4 6s. 81, balance of rent due from the 20th March to the 2nd July last. There was a counter claim, brought by Fellows, amounting to 19., for the use of a stye &c.—The case for the plain- tiff was conducted by Mr. Arthur Browne, nolicitor, of Warrington, whilst Mr. E. Brassey, solicitor, of Chester appeared fior Fellows. The story of the plaintiff was to the effect that in Oct- ober of 1893 he let a rmrtion of "Croten House," Halton to the defendant at a yearly rental of £l6 to be paid half yearly. An agreement was drawn up by the plain- tiff and consented to by the defendant. This agreement reserved to the plaintiff and also to his workmen,the right te pass through the yard in order to get to the workshop belonging to the plaintiff which adjoined " Croten House." An arrangement had previously been made t)e!- ween the parties, allowing a sow owned by plaintiff, to remain in one of Oa styes until she was fat enough to kill. Ako that a hencete should remain above this stye. Other little allowances of a similar nature were also alleged to have been arranged between them and agreed to by defendant. Owing to John Watkin, plaintiff's brother, being summoned on the 16th June last to that court to answer a charge of having assaulted Mrs. Fellows, which was believed to have arisen out of a dispute about this property,plaintiff coesumted to allow defendant to give up the house on the 210 July last. Mr. Burton, the solicitor for Mrs. Fellows, on tins occasion offered this settlement, and upon the recuammendation of his solicitor, Mr. Browne. be (plain- tiff) accepted it. The briefs of both legal gentlemen were accordingly signed : Mr. Burton's by Mr. Browne. land Mr. Browne's by Mr. Burton. The plaintiff had sent in his account amounting to £4 6s. al., by his brother, but the latter was told by the defendant that he would not pay anyone hut his brothar. Nothing was said about a counter claim. Subsequently the account was again sent in and the defendant answered it .by sending in the connter claim after he (plaintiff) had placed the rnatter in Mr. Browne's hands. The Defendant denied that he wffls liable for the £4 , 6s. Bd., and stated that his counter claim included an item for the housing of plaintiff's pig from the beginning of the tenancy to January this year. Tee occupation Juf the stye by the pig had been of much inconvenience to defendant, inasmuch as he had only agreed with the plaintiff to allow the animal to remain a fortnight instead of, as the plaintiff had just before stated, until she was fat enough to kill. Through the plaintiff refus- ing to take the pig away the defendant had not had sefficient room for other Pigs which he wished to put into the stye. The defendant also denied that he had arranged for the hencote to remain on his premises. This was one of the other items for which he had chart: .1 in his counter-claim. The plaintiff had lumbered up the yard of his house with some wheels and a machinery box, &c., which proved very inconvenient to defendant,. Two of his Pigs had broken their legs through these things being left in the yard. He understood, when he took the tenancyof the house that the yard was incheled. Ho had repeal eely requested the plaintiff to take the p,g, and hencete out of the stye and also the things which were in the yard, but to all these the landlord had sent, refusals. Further thin this, the defendant alleged that the plaintiff had borrewed several sacks from him,nearly twelve months ago, and had returned, in the place of them, after the action was brought, some that were aim )st worthlese—Being examined by Mr. E. Brasses', the plaintiff denied that he had let the yard to the defendant although it was mentioned in the agreement that a right of way was reserved. Flu' had a right to allow his wheels, and machinery box to lay there. He did not think it suffieiently important to mention in the written aereernenteanythin, shoot the pig being allowed to as in the shippon as well as the hencnte. Thee.' ar- rangements had been vtrbally made.—The defendant Fellows admitted to Mr. Browne in examinatinn that he had not once broached the matter of the counter claim or any of his grievances to Mr. William Watkin when he paid his rent. The landlord was always in such a hurry when he came that there appeared to he no time. It was not true that he haft started an action ler slander against the plaintiff ; nor haul he done so or told anynne that he had paid £2 towards a writ against the plaintiff. With that matter he had nothing whatever to do. although one of the partit s lodged at his house.—Mr. lirowne ex- pressed it as his opinion that the counter claim had been an afterthought with the defendant, subsequent to his hearing that these proceedings were being taken and was purely set no for spite. He thought it was only con- sistent with his client'a verbal agreement with the de- fendaet not to remove his pig and hencete. For these things the defend int in his counter claim, was charging really more than the very house was let to him for. The heuse wasonly Ga 2d.ner week.whereaa the defendant for the various things was charging more than 7s. per week. —II;e honour gave judgment for the plaintiff for the full amennt claimed with costs ; and for 2s. for the defend- ant for the detention of the sacks.

div.head: CONIPETITION IN TFIE IRON TRADE.
div.p: CONIPETITION IN TFIE IRON TRADE.

Speaking in response to the toast of his health at a social meeting at Brooklands, on Saturday even- ing, Mr. Thomas Morris, of the Pearson and Knowles Iron Co., Warrington, referred to his recent inve,tigations into the condition of the Bel- gium iron trade. He said that he had recently made a journey to Belgium to ascertain on the spot how it was they could make so cheaply this building and construction material which was imparted so largely into this country for building purposes. When he told them that in the Law Courts, London, there was used 11.000 tons of Beieitim iron, and in the Hotel Metropole 10.009 tons, they would have some idea, applying, it to the whole of England, of the enormous qtiantity of iron that came from Belgium. It had frequently puzzled him how they could beat us on our own ground, and he deterNined to ascertain the reason. He, fortunately, nvit in Antwerp a gentleman who was agyent fi7.r a Sheffield firm, who kindly volunteered to show him all that could be seen and give him every information pes- sible. He ascertained that the price of the pie iron at the works before it was made into those sections which architecrs were so fond of putting into our large build- ings was 35 francs, but that the Belgians had put a duty of six francs on French pig iron. The Belgians cried out because the French were sending pig iron into Belgium. In addition there were six francs per ton carriage, in all 50 francs, or £2, per ton. He (the speaker) said they got pig iron in England as cheap as that and thought it might be in the lower price of coal. The price, however, was as much as with us, and the price paid for pin-idling was the same. When he got to the woks he found that the puddlQrs who started with this pig iron were work- ing for a quarter the price we were paving in England to-day, and so on through every department it was a third or fourth less. 'These men worked almost con- tinuously for miserable wages. They knew nothing of a Sabbath or seventh day. In England the trades union leaders were cryini, out for an eight hours day, and while he did not desire that in England they should work longer than they did, some effort ought to be made whereby these men should have one day in seven, and something akin to the hours they had here. If they could not afford to pay more wages then they need not do it, but cut off these long hours, compel English rail- ways to carry merchandise at the same rate as they did in Belgium, and he did not think we should see one ton of building sections in England where now they saw thousands. He thought the trades union leaders and our workingmen should move to obtain shorter hours on the Continent, and then with fair rates of carriage and fair competition there would be more work and people would he happier all round. At the same time he wished it to he known in Belgium that what he saw there was sufficient to shame any man of common sense or any man who had capital to spend where labour was employed.

The misunderstanding at present existing with regard to the 10 per cent. reduction resulted in the miners em- ployed at the Bold Cellieries, St. Helens, refusing to ';'art work on Monday. They, in commen with the other miners of the district, fully agree to the reduction, but their ID air, object in not working was t, support, sixty or seventy lads employed in the mines to drive ponies. &c., from whom reductions were male. The colliers did net work on Saturday. On Monday moraine the colliers advised the lads not to. work, and this was agreed to, with the result that only four lads and fifty colliers out of a total 500, des- cended. Lite in the day. Mr. Jackson, the manager, was seen by a deput itien, and he impliei that he would not persist in the reduction. Acting on their decision at tee meeting on. Tuesday night, the lads firmly declined to descend the shaft of the Sherdley Colliery,owned by the White Cross Collieries Compeny.en Wednesday morning, and the result was that the 500 colliers employed ti-era had again to suspend operatiens for the day. The action of the Sherdley lade appears to have influenced the lads and young men employed at the Peaeley Cries Colliery, owned by the same firm, and they tee joined in the struggle on Wednesday morning by also refrring to des- cend the sh et of that pit. The dispute is a somewhat remarkable one, as the aggrieved young fellows assert that they are suffering mere than a 10 per cent. raduction, while the firm's manager, Mr. Turner, hes offered to submit the wages banks futile fecal miners' ofticials,amd in any case where it is pointed out or him that anyene; is :being . underpaielito at once make up the deficieece. In the -hope at inducing the • aggrieved lads to adopt a wiser course they were aeain. called together at the &lip Hotel, Riven-A', St. Helens, on Wednesday afternenn. Thera was a large attendance. and Mr. Peter IWKinley, who was chosen to preside, was supported by Mr. Pennington, Mr. Bradeury, and other members of a deputation who had helerviewed Mr. Turner, manager, and Mr. Carson, one of the managing directors of the firm, during the afternoon.— The Chairman reported that the depiration were re- eel ved in a frieedly manner, and both Mr. Carson and Mr. Turner seemed anxious te de everything' they could to redress the grievances nf the boys and the day wagemen without infringing the terms of the agreement come to through the Con- ciliation Board. A DIRTY CANAL BOAT. At the. Warrington Borough Court on Monday, a boat- au, named Robert Bell. of Barnton, was charged with :baying, on the 23rd July, been the mister of the canal boat "Thistle" registered as a dwelling boat, and failed to keep it in a cleanly condition. Inspector Norman stated that on the date named he visited the boat "Thisile" which was berthed at Bank Quay. He found the master's cabin in a very dirty Condition. The boat was also defective and the defendant was to blame for that, ecause he had not reported it to the Manchester Ship Canal Company, who owned the boat. Impector Powell stated that when he saw the defendant on the date named, he said that the boat got cleaned once a week whsther it wanted it or not. One cabin was in a very dirty condition. When the deck was washed, the water ran through into the cabin. It, was the first time therdefendaat had come to Warrington. A fine of 53. including costs was imposed. CHARGE AGAINST A FISH DEALER. At the Borough Police Court yesterday-,Wm. Bottotnl7 fishmonger, Naylor-St., was summoned at the instance of Inspector Norman, for having exposed for sale 58 herrings, 109 bloaters, 164 kippers, and 39 lbs. of findon haddock, which was unfit for human food. Mr. A. Browne, solicitor, represented the defendant. Inspector Norman stated that on Saturday, the 21st July, at abut twenty minutes to twelve, he was in the market inspecting fish. When he came to Mr. Bottomley's stall he 'found thirteen boxes of fish lying with a barrel of berrings against the stall. Witness examined them,and Pound seven boxes zontaining the fish mentioned in the charge, which was unfit for food. Mrs. Bottomlea came up, and wanted to put the fish in a tank which was close to the stall, stating that the fish was not intended for sale. The fish was sent to the Medical Officer who after examining it declared it unfit for food. Witness 'afterwards sAw Bottomley who asked him to be as lenient as ia e could with him that time,and he would see that it did not occur again. Mr. Browne stated that on ' the:date named the weather was very hot. The defend- ant 'had done business in the market for 20 years, and had never previously had anything brought against him. On, this occasion he went to Manchester and bought 15 cwt of fresh fish which he sent by train. He was taken ill pd went home to bed. He, however, instanced his asiistant to take the fish, which was left in stock tram the previous day. and put it in tanks provided for off d atthe market. The assistant, instead of putting it in the tank, placed it near to it with the intention of doing so, audit was there when the Inspector found it. William Deliy.ze corroborated Mr. Browne's statement, and said he was called away when he was about to put the fish in the tank. The sound fish which was on the stall hail besi,n bought the same morning at Manchester. The sWjk 9aid the defendant was liable to a penalty of £7;400. The chairman said the law had been broken am* someone was rf sponsible for it. The defendant watad be fined £1 and costs. 44:

div.head: SELECTION OF THE SITE.
div.p: SELECTION OF THE SITE.

The provision of a much-needed public cemetery for the borough of Widnes advanced another stage at the monthly meeting of the Widnes Town Coun- cil held on Tuesday afternoon. For over twelve months a special committe of the Council have had the matter under their consideration, and, after an exilathtive inquiry, they came to the conclusion that a public cemetery was needed in the town, and they sub- mitted a report to the Town Council to this effect. The Council unanimously adopted this report, and the matter was then referred to the General purposes and Parlia- mentary Committee, to select a suitable site. Several 'tenders were received in answer to the advertisement for sites, and these have been under corsideration of the committee for the past two months. report was submitted to the Town Council on Tuesday. and stated that. Messrs. White, Maclver, and Co. offered to a,;cept £5,000 for the portion of Moss Brook estate lying to the north of the Cheshire Lines nilw,sy (other than the cottages), and estimated to contain 49 acres or there- abouts. The corismittee, having considered statements as to the rentals arising trom the property, resolved that it was desirable, in the interests of the borough, to acquire the whole of the land offered, not withstanding that the arra thereof was greater than wajs quired for present cemetery purposes, and that, sitt,j,ct to the conditions named, the offer be accepted. The committee also decided that it was not nece-sary for the Town Council to take any steps under the Burials Act, 1854, for vesting in the Council powers for providing places of burial under the Act.—Alderman Wareing. in proposing that the minutes be confirmed, said the committee received sixteen offers of land. The Moss Brook Site, he thought, was a very suitahle one. It was in a good state of cultivation, it was central, it stood high, and was in close proximity to a Corporation sewer.—Coun- cillor Ownes seconded.—Councillor Christie thought the provision of a cemetery was premature.—Councillor Neil agreed with the previous speaker.—Councillor Shores opposed the Act under which the committee were moving, and quoted a large number of statistics with the object of showing that it would be more satisfactory and economical to take steps under the Burials Act instead of the Public Health Act, which the committee intended to proceed under. He moved an amendment that the second resolution be referred back to a commit, tee of the whole Council.—Counciilor Smith seconded the amendment.—Alderman Wareing having replied, the amendment was lost by 14 votes t 4 5, and the minutes were afterwards confirmed.

. BUBSTED JUNE 1894. Ben Bearings aas a bicyclist Who never tyreci of teer, Got so intl-rted that he was Most always out of gear. And when it mounted to his head, The sockets ot his eyes Got hollow-rimmed, and he would brake The welkin with his cries. And yet indeed he was no crank, He oft would frame a Hie, And when not chained to bar, then his Direct in-tension spoke ! He'd brake the record frequently And never use his brake ! And though he lampooned everyone, His lamp he'd seldom take! He skidded tandem through the world, And when steered clear of pubs, His guard and lamp (his wife) would say He was the best of hubs. Sound the alarm ! Beh's wind is gone ! He's punctured wide and deep, Let's hope he is not scorching now, Poor Benjy's gone to sleep.
