div.head: 3HE DIVISION OF WESTON TOWNSHIP
div.p: 3HE DIVISION OF WESTON TOWNSHIP
INTO WARDS.

COUNTY COUNCIL INQUIRY. A Committee of the Cheshire County Council comprising Messrs. W. R. Earp, H. Nield, and P Speakman, J.P., raft on Tuesday in the National School, Weston Point, to cowider a memorial signed by more than one-tenth of the ratepayers of the township of Weston, and approved at a public meeting that the township be divided into two wards for the purpose of the election of parish councillors. The attendance included the Rev. D. S. Bowen. Messrs. E. Aaron, T. Ford (overseers), J. Collier (assistant over- seer), L. Rosenberg, T. Handley, J.P., J. Ford, T. T. Sill, J. Hammerslev, J. Vose, 'l'. Griffiths, Cookson, W. Handley, and Pickering, with Mr. Potts, clerk to the Cheshire County Council. Mr. Earp having explained why the inquiry had been
instituted, Mr. Potts read the memorial in which the reasons for the proposal were stated and setting forth the conveni- ence such a division would be to the residents of Weston

Point. The Rev. D. S. Bowen, who explained that he had been asked to state the case of the committee appointed at the public meeting, now described the boundaries of the proposed Weaver ward. The boundary line started from the stone cranes, round the lane up to the road, then down the road to the left hand side until Handley's smithies were reached (these houses not being taken in). From thence about fifty yards up the road, where there was a path straight through the fields until they came to the boundary of Runcorn. Then in a straight line to Delamere Dock completed the boundary. Continuing, he said that all the people in that radius came to Weston Point to do their shopping, and they all went to church or chapel and sent their children to school in the Weston Point portion of the township. This showed that the inhabitants resident therein were quite distinct from Weston. The population at the census of 1891 was set at 2,339 and according to the particulars contained in the diocesan calander, Weston Point was given 864 show- ing that the Weston ward would comprise 1,475 people. When the census was taken the Ship Canal works were in operation and 20 huts were erected in the district each one containing from 10 to 15 inhabitants. Then there were 10 vessels in dock with an average in each. He allowed a reduction of 250 from toe regular residents, thus bringing the population in Weaver ward to 614. From a census which he himself had recently taken, he found that since 1891 the population had increased by 246, so that the present number stood at 860. In Weston there were 1,475 residents when the census was taken. The Alkali works were then in full swing, and he had been given to understand,that. such was not the case now. The quarrymen were then working full time,stone being required for the construction of the canal. But now that undertaking had been completed. The promoters of the selietne claimed that the population of Weston ward had decreased by 450 persons. (Laughter.) Mr. Collier remarked that there was not a single empty house in the village. The Rev. D. S. Bowen argued that the Weaver ward was increasing whilst Weston was decreasing. He had further been given to understand that the Salt Union was going to increase their working capacity in that district; and if they doubled the number of pans it would mean labour for 137 extra men. The Railway Company were already laying down a double set of rails at the lay-by to meet the demand for the extra produc- tion of salt. The people of Weaver ward were unani- mously in favour of the scheme, and after holding a public meeting and appointing three representatives to meet the County Council Committee at Runcorn to make their claims, they forwarded a petition to the County Council. The rev, gentleman believed that the salt Company favoured the division: and Captain Clarke,the largest individual ratepayer in the neighbourhood, had just expressed his sympathy with the scheme by tele- graph, and regretted his inability to be present. Unless they got the Weaver ward they would be disenfranchised. Speaking about the probability of an electicn contest,he said that he for one did not think there would be one, as they had worked together harmoniously in the past. But even if such were to turn out the case, surely a it in the £ was not too much to enable workingmen to have the opportunity of taking part in local government. Mr. Potts inquired from Mr. Collier what the rateable value was of Weston Point. Mr. Collier answered that it was £4,500; and that of Weston, £7,947. In the prop-used Weaver ward there were 179 houses against 300 in Weston. He was unable

to give the acreage. Mr. James Ford believed that the townships consisted of between 800 and 700 Cheshire acres,or of 1.500 statute acres. 'The number of acres in each ward he did not kenw. Mr. Sill thought that Weston embraced fully two-thirds pf the entire township. Mr. Potts observed that of the questions for considera- tion one was the allocation of the Parish Councillors if the Council decided to divide the township. The scale entitled Weston to thirteen parish councillors ; and the committee wished for the opinion of the meeting as to how that number should be divided between Weston and Weaver wards. The Rev. D. S. Bowen first suggested that Weston be given the majority of one, but afterwards he intimated that the inhabitants of Weston Point would be satisfied if five councillors were given them and the remaining eight apportioned to Weston. In answer to Mr. Aaron, the Rev.D.S.Bowen said that the ratepayers' meeting he had spoken of was held in the same room in which they were now assembled. Mr. Aaron said there had not ben a ratepayers meet- ing in Weston, nor could there be a legal one called without its being called by the overseers. Mr. Ford and himself had first heard of the meeting through a paper. Neither did lie know that the memorial was being got up: He further questioned whether those at the meeting were ratepayers seeing that the River Weaver Navigation paid the rates. The Rev. D.S. Bowen asked why the overseers had not convened a meeting, and afterwards referred to the advice given them at the inquiry at Runcorn. Mr. Potts explained that the inquiry alluded to.simply referred to the Board of Guardians and not to the divi- sion of the townships into wards. Notices of the inquiry were sent to all the overseers in the county asking that if they intended making any application to the Council for the division of their tow st ships into wards they were to send them in at once. None was, however, received from Weston. Mr. Aaron said that at the meetings held in Weston the ratepayers did not present themselves. A few weeks ago they convened a meeting to consider the counts, rate basis but not a single person was present front Weston Point. Mr. Potts remarked that the reason he supposed for this was that the Weaver Navigation paid the rates. Mr. Aaron, after saying that they had tried hard to keep the rates down, added that the last election cost £25 and if they were to have a contest in two places it would mean £5O, or id. in the £ en the rates. Mr. Potts said it was impossible for anyone present to sly how much the additional eost would be, because no ' scale of •charges had yet been issued by the Local Government Board or the Counts, Council. Mr. Rosenberg stated that- although the navigation paid the rates, the money came out of the servants' pockets, and they were therefore entitled to votes. Mr. Potts observed that if there was any doubt about the legality of the meeting he would like to know whether the memorial had been signed by one-tenth of the pArochial electors. The Rev. D. S. Bowen replied that it contained the signatures of more than one-tenth of the people,and they obtained them because the overseers would not call a meeting. Mr. Aaron said that if the Rev. D.S. Bowen had Rent a note with a petition from so many ratepavere of Weston Point asking for a tneeting tc be convened', the overseers were bound to do it, Mr. Ford also stated that the overseers received no notice of the meeting. Mr. Earp explained that the people of Weston Point had fulfilled the requirements of the law by sending a signed petition. Mr. Aaron denied that the population of Weston had be.en reduced since 1891, and stated that not a single house was to be seen "to let" in the village. Mr. James Moore in supporting the scheme, said that the inhabitants had been kept in the dark with regard to the working of the Local Government Act. The Weaver ward was composed of hard working people, and unless something was done they would not reap the advan- tages offered by the measure. Mr. Rosenberg, after saying that as a Weaver naviga- tion servant he was always anxious to keep down the rates, added that he had -Mr. Imison's authority to see that whatever was required in the interest of the be " Trust "should be carried out. It would not be well, thought,if the Parish Council work was all transacted at Weston. The meetings should be held alternately in each village.because there were men employed by the "Trust" to whom it would he a convenience. Mr. T. Handles J.P. understood that a strong feeling had for some time existed in Weston Point because of their not possessing any representation on the Board of IGuardians. The nominees from Weston village had always been carried, and he thought the natural situa- tion of the villages showed that they should be divided into wards. The interests of both villages were different and quite separate. The theory of representation was that all parties should be represented ; and if Weston Point was not divided into a ward this would not thoroughly be the case. Mr. Potts said it had already been decided to grant the township two guardians. Now,if it was divided as pro: posed, was it desired that there should be one for each ward, or elect the two by the township at large? Mr. T. Handley : One for each ward. The Salt Union are going to enlarge their works and they will increase the rateable value ' • whereas at Weston it is decreasing. Mr. Sill denied that there had been any decrease in the ropulation of Weston. No resident had left the, works. Nearly all the men who had been suspended had come from a distance. Some of the people in favour of the scheme, he thought, were under the impression that there would be a parish meeting in each. Mr. Potts explained that there would only be one parish meeting in each township, but the representatives would be elected from each ward. In reply to Mr.

Rosenberg he said the place of meeting would be a matter for subsequent settlement. Mr. Sill thought that as there would only be two days in the year when the electors would have to visit Wes- ton, it would not be a very great hardship if the request was not acceded to. Weston contained fully two-thirds of the population and that was the extent of its rateable value ; and the residents there were quite willing that every third year the meeting and election should take place at Weston Point. By this they would suffer no in- ' justice. Why he opposed the division was the extra ex- pense it would incur, seeing that the separation was not necessary. They were even prepared to allow the meetings to take place at Weston Point every alternate year. Mr. Potts: lam afraid you cannot bind your suc- cessors. _ _

Mr. Speakman : It shows your good feeling towards them. (Laughter.) He said it was very nice to find them all so friendly and combined in keeping down the rates. Mr. James Ford considered that it was not desirable that so small a village should be divided into two parts. No resident would have to go more than a mile if it was necessary to go from one extreme of the village to the other; and it would be a folly to have two polling booths.

Mr. T. Ford said he took the position of guardian with reluctance, and he had told the assistant overseer, if one were nominated from Weston Point, to withdraw his (Mr. Fords) name. The Committee then retired for a few minutes and on returning Mr. Earp announced that they had considered the subject fully and could not help coming to the con- clusion that it was desirable to divide the township into wards. They would recommend the Council to make on order for the division, and to allocate five Councillors to the Weaver ward, and eight to the Weston ward, with one guardian or district Councillor for each ward. He thought the characteristics of the two townships were altogether distinct. On the proposition of Mr. Aaron, seconded by Mr. Rosenberg,a vote of thanks was passed to the committee for exercising so much care and attention to the matter. The proceedings then terminated.

div.p: RUNC.''ORN SCHOOL BOARD.

THE BOARD AND TECHNICAL INSTRUCTION. Mr. J. Pritchard presided over the monthly meet- ing of this Board which was held on Tuesday even- ing in the Town Hall, Runcorn. The other gentle- men present were the Rev. Or. Gastaldi, Dr. McDougall, Messrs. S. Taylor, J.P., T. Handley, J.P., R. Imison, and G. Moss (clerk.)

THE PROVISION OF SCHOOL ACCOMMODATION. The Clerk read the report of the Committee appointed on March 6th to consider the subject of providing school accommodation in place of the Wesleyan Schools which were to be closed or transferred to the Board a few weeks ago, but which the managers have decided to con- tinue for another year. The report stated that "On March 6th a letter was addressed to the Wesleyan mana- gers asking upon what terms they proposed to transfer their schools to the Board. In reply the Committee were informed that the trustees of the Brunswick School (Boys) did not desire either to sell or to let these schools permanently to the Board as they were required for church and Sunday school purposes. Granville-st. schools (Girls and Infants) not being required for similar purposes, it was the intention of the trustees to sell them and they were offered in the first place to the School Board. In considering this offer the Committee was met with the difficulty that the Education Department pro- nounced the schools to be unfit for maintenance by the Board. For' temporarily, it must be under section 23 of the Act 1870 which provided, that for the transfer t ) the i School Board a voluntary school should have received building grants. Stich schools must be transferred, free of any charge either of rent or purchase, otherwise the Department would not recognise them as Board Schools. The Wesleyan managers from the outset declined to transfer on these terms, and the Committee has had some anxiety about the provi- , sion of the accommodation in case the schools were closed. But this has been set at rest by the managers deciding to continue them for a further period of twelve months. Since this decision the committee has written fully to the Educational Department in order to ascertain definitely what can be done with respect to the schools alluded to, and the answer was conveyed in the following letter from the department, dated June 12th :—' Adverting to your letter dated 31st ult., lam directed to refer your Board to paragraph 2 of 96 8., and I am to state that my Lords cannot recogni.e the Granville school as a Board school unless it is transferred under section 23 of the Elementary Education Act of 1870. As my I.4u•ds understand that the managers are not prepared to transfer the schools under that section it seems unnecessary to enter into the question whether the school could be rendered tit for permanent use by the School Board. The Board should lese no time in obtaining a site for building a new school to supply the deficiency of school accommodation which will be caused by the closing of the Wesleyan Schools. A plan of the site which the Board selects, drawn to a scale of forty feet to an inch, and showing its boundaries and abuttals should be submitted to the department for approval with a statement of the number of children (boys, girls and infants respectively) for whom it is proposed to build.' Having respect to the communication from the Education Department it will be necessary for the Boar.) to provide the requisite accommodation consequent upon the closing of the Wesleyan Schools." The report of the committee was adopted. The Chairman said it would be necessary for the work of the committee to he continued and accordingly pro- posed the re-appointment of the whole Board as the com- mittee to proceed with the question of the provision of school accommodation through the closing of the Wes- leyan schools. The proposition was seconded by,Mr. Handley and carried. THANKS TO THE WESLEYAN SCHOOL MANAGERS. Dr. McDougall proposed that the thanks of the Board he given to the managers of the Wesleyan Day Schools for coming to their aid by continuing the schools for another year. The public of Runcorn were indebted to the managers of the Wesleyan schools for coming to their rescue at a time when the Board were in a difficulty,and he thought that this expression of thanks was due to them. Mr. Taylor seconded with much pleasure, saying that he telt sure they all felt grateful to the managers for the twelve month's grace which would enable them (the Board) to make proper provision. The Chairman supported the motion, endorsine, all the remarks that had l,ieen passed.—The proposition was carried unanimously. , THE SCIENCE AND ART CLASSES.

Mr. Moss read a letter which had been written to the Runcorn Improvement Commissioners in accordance with the wishes of the Science and Art Classes Com- mittee in which he had stated that as it seemed likely that the Technical Institute would be completed during the autumn the Committee presumed that the Board would desire to have the classes under their manage- ment as soon as the rooms were ready. If so it would be advisable for them to undertake the work from Sep- tember. If necessary it could be arranged for the Com- missinners to have the use of the Greenway-road schools. —A reply to this communication had been received from Mr. E. Marshall, secretary which ran as follows I am directed by the Technical Instruction Cemmittee to say that they had considered the matter and resolved to request the School Board to carry on the Science and Art classes for the forthcoming winter and they would be happy to hand over the Technical Institute when completed, for the use of the classes during the ensuing session if they so desired. The com mittee fully appre- ciated the good work done by the School Board in that direction, and the members hoped that they would sea their way to carrying on their valuable labours for an- other year." Dr. Mc Dougall remarked that the Board must feel highly flattered by such a request from the Technical Instruction Committee. Mr. Imison proposed that the wish of the committee be acceded to. Although he had felt inclined at first to oppose the request because he had considered some ob- servations made were not of the kindest character. he now thought that there had been no intention to reflect upon the Board's manner of conducting the work. If the Board did not carry on the work, however, a large number of students would be placed in a difficulty, as it was always easier to disperse a class than to form one. It would also be disadvantageous to the students to dis- continue their studies for a period. Therefore, he pro- posed that the Board undertake the formation of the classes and the routine work to be done. The Rev. Dr. Gastaldi in seconding the motion, said that he hoped the Board would do all in their power to make the Science and Art classes successful.as the work was highly beneficial to tlse youth of the town. Dr. McDougall in referring to what had been said by Mr. Imison, remarked that the observations that that gentleman had heard with regard to the manner in which the Board had carried on their work were unjusti- fied especially seeing that the Science and Art Classes Committee consisted of the School Board and the Corn- nessioners. The Board had performed their duties in that direction to the best of their ability, and a spirit of gratefulness prevailed seeing that the committee had saved £6OO which should be expended on the classes. He thoueht it unbecoming that tkeir actions should be criticised and that they should be told that they had not grasped the situation. The cammittee had done a good work, which was not sought by the Board, and the members experienced satisfaction by knowing what a number of students had passed. Dr. Gastaldi advised the Board to take no further cognizance of the matter than the letter sent in by the Board which was very courteous and gratifying. Mr. Imison said it had been an unfortunate reference by him. The proposition was then carried and the public pro- ceedings terminated.

John Yonge was the chairman. He said ho wag thankful to see such a full church that aftvrnoon. TheP.S.A. mettlngs had found their place in the hearts of the pc.-.-ople. The fact t,,at so many lady friends had come to that quarterly meeting was a sign that they were tharileul that those meetings had been commenced in the town. Mrs. Renton, of Frodsham, delivered the address for the afternoon. She laid before her hearers the importance of deciding for Christ, and engaging in Christi. n work. Mrs. 11-nton also contributed a solo. v! Arm, atm ye brave " Was the title of a solo given by Mr. W. H. Wallington, and Miss Frances Booth sang "Satl. in the arms of Jesus." Mr. W. H. ATHLETICS.
CRICKET.

Warrington, 126 ; Manchester, 219 for nine wickets ! This result must have been a great disappointment to the supporters of tile Warrington team. It was hoped that, alter their fine form at Llandudno the previous week, Warrington would have been able to rep-at their performance of last year by defeating the Mancurians on their own turf. But no ! whatever the Warrington team were able to do last year, they seem unable to sus- tain it this season. There is this, however, to be said in their favour, that the Manchester team was an excep- tionally strong one, including as it did, six professionals whose names have figured at one time or other in the Lancashire county eleven, whilst on the other hand the Warrington team was but of the ordinary strength.

The County ground at Old Trafford was the scene of operations, and the turf was in fine condition. War- rington were the first to show their ability with the willow, and the commencement was very encouraging— not to the Warrington batsmen, oh no ! but to the Man- chester bowler, Hallam, for with his sieond ball he dis- turbed Mr. R. Smith's wickets. After this reverse, Warrington's prospects brightened a little on the partner- ship of Bates and Wordsworth,but they were not of long duratiw, for when nineteen runs had been score(' ,Tinsley, who was at one time professional for Warringten,by a fine catch, disposed of the present Warrington professional, and with only four more runs notched, Wordsworth was caught. Not daunted by this series of reverses the two succeeding batsmen, S.M. Crosfield, and J. Callon, set to work in dswnright earnest. Callon struck out vigorowly, and seemed determined to eclipse his score of 60. made the Saturday previous. The home team found it neces- sary to call into requisition fresh bowlers.but this had no deterring effect on the two batsmen, for when lunch- time arrived they were still together, and the score had crept up to 64.

On the resumption of hostilities, the valuable stand which had been made by Messrs. S. M. Crosfield and J. Callon was brought to a conclusion, for ten more runs had only been added when Crosfield was bowled by Hallam. G. Clarke followed on, but he was as unfor- tunate as R. Smith, for two balls were sufficient to send him back to the pavilion. The other Clark, who suc- ceeded him, was more successful, and made a good partner to Callon, who still scored at a rapid pace, pay- , ing little respect to the repeated changes in the bowling. Ile continued in this style until 106 was reached, when he was caught by Tickle. His score was 63, and there was much cheering on his departure. It is the higheA score he has made for Warrington this season, and the Widnesian's performance was theevent of the match,his score including no fewer than eight fours. The remain- ing batmen did not add many runs, and the venture closed for 126.

The Manchester team commenced their innings with the brothers MacLaren, but they had only compiled 12 runs when the well-known A. C. MacLaren was clean bowled by J. J. Cro,field, and at 33 the other brother was caught at the boundary. 11. Tinsley and Rowley hit out with much freedom, and the former compiled 28, and the latter 42, before being caught. The Wairington bowling wilt severely punished by the succeeding bats- men, as evidenced by the fact, that all of them, with one exception reached double figures. When the score had reached 219, play was stopped. Manchester still having another wicket to fall. -

Whilst the first team was suffering defeat at Man- chester, the second team very narrowly escaped faring as bmily on their ground at Arpley. Their opponents were the 2nd eleven of Broughton, and it was the first meeting of the two clubs. A most promising start was made by the visitors, for before the first wicket had fallen, the initial batsmen had scored 74. By goxl play this was augmented to 206 for the loss of nine wickets, Tinker being the highest contributor with 52 to his credit. , 'Towards the visitor's formidable score,Warrington made a very feeble display. At seven o'clock,the time for dis- continuing play, they had only compiled 60 runs for the loss of seven wickets. Thus it will be seen that time alone saved them from an almost certain defeat. Toe Broughton captain must have repented not having de- clared his innings cicsed earlier in the match.

A very even match was played at Si-. Helens, on Saturday, between the Sankey Bridges Wesleyans and the St. Helens Congregationals. The former scored 41 and the latter 39. Singularly, each team owes more than half its score to the skill of one man. Peers, for the Wesleyans, carried his bat throulh for 29, whilfi Robinson for St. Helens,onlv gave in when he had com- piled the respectable total of 21.

On Saturday the Orford Barracks sergeants were cornpelled to acknowledge that their " mettle" was not quite equal to that turned out by the Sankey Wire Mill 3. their resistance to the visitors' bowling was somewhat feeble, as only two of their number, Casolani and Kirk, made anything like a decent show. Williams, Cook,and Woodcock contributed largely to the 183 complied by the Wire Mills. The match was in fact decided be- fore the fall of their sixth wicket, as the soldiers only managed to make 83.

The Fairfield team had a very easy timo of it on Saturday, as the only work they were called upon to do was to "play" with the bowling of the Cemetery White Rose, and afterwards to dismiss for only 11 runs, the whole of the latter team. For their own side the Fair- &Ad men scored 60 for 6 wickets, of which the Molest individual scores were made by Whittaker and Eyre. These two also had the honour of doing all the bowling necessary to drive the Cemetery men from the wickets.

The Chesh're Lines Engineers cricket team ccom- pulled by about twelve friends left Warrington at ten o'clock on Saturdiv morning for Burton which was reached at noon, when, by the kind permission of thB mana.:4er (4f Tlsre. Allsops, brewers, they were con- ducted throu,4ll their brewer.-. A match was afterwarls played agaimit the Horton M.R.C.C., in which the Cheshire Lines Engineers defeated the M.R.C.C. by 90 runs and one wicket. The engineers batted first ano with the total at 127 for 9 wickets closed their innint:s. Howard,t;cott,lrvinm,and Deeley were the top soorer.4 for the winn,.rs. The M.R. were dismissed for 37 runs ow- ing to the splendid bowling of Monks, who Nok five wickets for 18 runs. Harrison secured 4 for 16 runs. The engineers then returned home,Warrington being reached at 10.35 after a most enloyable day's outing.
ATIILETICS.

I was glad to see that at the Radcliffr! C.C. sport, on- Saturciay, J. Buxton, Warrington, secured third ulace in the two mile bicycle race, and that in the quarter mile raceJ. Fair, Warrington, with 34 yards start, came in second. A. I'. Daintith,of Warrington. was also success- ful in the mile bicycle race, with 155 yards start, at Birkenhead. Well done Warrington cyclists !

div.head: CYCLING.
div.p: CYCLING.

About half a doz9n members of the Warrington Cycl- ing Club, started on Saturday, for a tour through North '4'ales. The route pa4sed through (TheAter, L'angoilen, Corwen, Llandudno, and Barmouth. Llandudno was reached on Mondav,and up to that time the weather had been exceedingly pleasant, there being an entire absence of rain. They wore expected to arrive at B,trrnOuth on Thursday. A better cycling tour than this through North Wales, could hardly be found, for in beauty of scenery it is unequalled. True I it is rather hilly,but what does a cyclist care about hills if his wind is good and he knows there is a substantial " feed" to wreak venge- ance on, at the other end. 'I he troop is expected back to-day.
THE GLASS TRADE OF ST. HELENS.

IMPENDING STOPPAGE OF WORKS. On Wednesday afternoon the following notice was posted at the Ravenhead and Sutton Plate Glass Works, St. Helens, belonging to the London and Manchester Elate Gass Company :—" Owing to the great depres- sion in their trade the directors have N intimate that on and after Thursday next, the 23rd inst., all persons em- ployed by the company will be retained from day to day only until further notice, August 15th, 1894." This notice will enable the company to discharge any of their employe., immediately after the date mentioned. It is not known exactly whether any general or partial stoppage will take placc, as the officials at the works maintain strict silence on tne subject. Rumour, however, has been busy lor a long time respecting the works in (vie., tion, it being stated that the company were losing- £1,500 a week. No dividend bias been paid for a number of years. It is understood a meeting of the directors will be held in Manchester next week,when some definite de- cision will be come to. B-.‘tween 700 and 800 men are employed at the Sutton works and between 300 and 400 at Ravenhead. The Ravenhead Glassworks is the oldest in Lancashire. P was erected by a company which was established in 1793, French workmen being employed to introdw.e the indirstry. On its failure the concern was transferred in 1798 to a new company, and it was the produce of this concern which rendered the British plate glass famous. Since then, however, the firm of Messrs. Pilkinv,ton Bros. has sprung into existence, and has long , since held the lead in Lancashire and in England for the extent and variety of its output.

div.head: JOHN WARRINGTON OFF TO GAOL
div.p: JOHN WARRINGTON OFF TO GAOL
AGAIN.

That notorious foundling, John Warrington, was again placed in the dock at the Borough Police Court. on Wednesday morning, to answer a charge preferred against him by the police. His attire was fir from being attractive, for it consisted solely of a sugar sack. This unusual dress, it afterwards trans- pired, had been provided him by the police, for during his incarceration in the cells the previous night, he, for some unexplained reason, tore his clothes into shreds. He had been placed in custody in consequence of infor- mation which ereehed the police on Tuesday morning. Early that day " John" had made his way to the house of Mr. Hesketh, 3, Wilsan Patten-st. On Mrs. Hesketh going into the bathroom about 11-30 a.m. she was staztled to find him busily washing his hands. She at once asked him what he was doing there, but he was quite equal to the occasion, and told her that Mr. Hes- keth had sent him there to wash his hands. Mrs. Hes- keth, thinking that he had been doing some work for her husband, believed his story, and left the room,allowing him to finish his ablutions. Soon afterwards, however, she saw him standing at the top of the stairetnear to one of the bedroom doors. In answer to another question she put to him, he 'replied that he was waiting for Mr. Hesketh. " John " did not wait any longer, for while Mrs. Hesketh went to tell her husband, he rushed out of the house by the front door. Mr.Hesk,th,on being informed of tile occurrence was greatly surprised,far he had not seen the young man,nor did he know anything at all ‘about him. The police were at once in- formed, and from the description given, John Warring- ton was arrested in Corporation-st. the same morning by P.C. Turner. He was taken to the Police Station, placel amongst four other persons, and Mrs. Hesketh was brougnt to see if she could identify the person she had found in her house. She at once pointed out Warring- ten, she having noticed that his lower lip was split in the centre. Ile was searched but only a knife and wrench were found upon him. The magistrates who tried him the following morning were Messrs. J. Geddes and J. H. Fleming. On being charged with being a con- victed thief found on the enclosed premises of 3, Wilson Patten-st., the previous morning for the unlawful pur- pose of committing a felony, the prisoner in a loud voice shouted" not guilty." Evidence bearing out the above account was given by Mr. and Mrs. Hesketh, P.C. Turner, and Inspector Spiiiks. Mrs. Hesketh deposed that nothing had been missed from the house. Mr. Hes- keth stated that the only way he could account for the prisoner getting into the house unnoticed was, that the servants were washing downstairs, and the back door being open, the prisoner must have entered without being seen by them. Tie magistrates committed the prisoner to gaol for three months hard labour. On hearing the sentence Warrington used most obscene lan- guage stating that he could do that on his head. He al,io used fearful threats as to what he would do when he came out again. Mr. li%eming was of the opinion that the prisoner should be sent out of the country. Mr. Geddes thought that it would be better to put the pri- soner in an asylum.

div.head: FATAL CARRIAGE _ACCIDENT NEAR
div.p: FATAL CARRIAGE _ACCIDENT NEAR
IRLAV. THE MAIL CART IN COLLISION.

About eleven o'clock on Saturday evening a car- riage accident, attended with fatal results,occurred on the Nlanchester and Liverpool highway near Ir- lam. It appears that the Gavernment mail cart, while passing round a curve on the road near Foxhill, came iuto violent collision with a carriage containing four gentlemen from Eccles. The whole of the occupants were thrown from the vehicle., and Mr. George Thomp- son, of Lorne Villas, Wellington-road, received injuries of so severe a nature that he died shortly afterwards. Mr. Richard Garside, also of Lorne Villas, Wellington- road, Mr. Hardman and Mr. Weir, the other occupants of the vehicle, were likewise injured more or less seriously. 'Die driver of the mail cart, Charles Davidsan, was apprehended on his return from Warrington by Inspector O'Hara and placed in the police cells at Peri- croft, where he was formally charged with being drunk and incapable whilst in custody of the mail cart. At the Manchester County Police Court. on Monday, George Davison, mail ceach driver, of Park-st., Cheet- ham, was placed in the dock on a charge of being drunk in charge of three horses and a mail coach at Patricroft. There was also a further charge against him of having caused the death of George Thompson, at Irlam, on the 11th inst.—Mr. Superintendent Bent said he only pro- posed to go into the first charge that day. The ir4queste on the deceased man would he held on Tuesday, and he asked that the.prisoner should be remanded.—Mr. Yates said he thought it would be better to adjourn both cases.—Mr. Hockin, who defended, said he was quite agreeable to such a course.—ln answer to the Bench, Mr. Bent stated that it was alleged that Davison was drunk when in charge of a mail coach, and that he ran into a carriage containing four gentle- men. The vehicle yas upset and one of the gentle- men was killed.—The prisoner was remanded for a week.—Mr. Elockin askel for bail. He stated that the prisoner was a householder. He denied being drunk, and said that the unfortunate affair was an accident. The accused desired to he present at the inquest.—Mr. Bmt offered no objection, and the bench -fixed the bail at two sureties of £25 each and himself in £lOO. The County Groper (Mr. F. Price) opened an inquiry at Eccles on fuesda v, into the circumstances attending the death of Mr. George Thompson. It is alleged that the driver of the mail coach was under the influence of drink at the time of the accident, but this is denied by the man who was in charge of the vehicle. It came out in evidence that on Saturday evening the mail coach had more than one strange adventure, for after colliding with the dogcart occupied by Mr. Thompson and his companions it ran over a man who was lying in the middle of the roadway. The inquest was a- joorned until Thursday for the attendance of some witnesses. • The inquest was resumed, before Mr. F. Price, coroner at the Cross Keys Hotel, Eaclea, on Thursday morning. The inquest waa primarily adjourned for the attendance of a witness who,it was reported,had actually witnessed the accident. The Coroner said that this man had been interviewed, and he said be knew nothing about the occurrence. Therefore he had not been summoned. After hearing the evidence of several witnesses, chiefly confirmatory of that adduced at the first hearing, the jury decidad not to adjourn for the evid,,ne, of Garaida, another occupant of tha trap at the time of the collision as it is not expected he will he ante to leave the house for sever.il weeks. The Coroner then addressed the jury and explained to them that if they considered Davidson in an unfit state to take charge of the horsea,and that it, owing to his earel,-es driving that Mr. Girside's trap was °versa and Mr. Thampson killed, it would he their duty to return a verdict of manslamhter against him. The jury retired, and after a few minutes' consultation re- I turned a verdict of "accidental death."

MOTHERS! MOTHERS! to know that a single application of the CUTICUttA REMEDIR:twiII afford instant relief, permit rest and sleep, and point to a speedy and economical cure of torturing, disfiniring, itching, burn- ing, and scaly humours, and not to use them without a moment's delay is to fail in your duty. Cures made in infancy an i childhood are speedy, permanent, and eco- nomical. Truly, CUTICURA WORKS WONDERS, and its cures of torturing, disfiguring, humiliating humours are the most wonderful ever recorded in this or any age.

div.head: WARRINGTON.
div.p: WARRINGTON.
ACCIDENT AT THE CENTRAL STATION.

On MOntlay n.lorning, an elderly lady named Mrs. Bates, trom Sheffield, was stet.pina out of the train from Sheffield at the Central Station at Warrington, when she zilipped and fell on the platform, injuring her knee rather severely. She was immediately conveyed on stretchers to the Infirmary by the rail- way officials.

div.head: DEATH OF AN OLD TRADESMAN.
div.p: DEATH OF AN OLD TRADESMAN.

The death of Mr. John IVainwright, took place after a very short illnesQ, at his residence, Bntter- market-street, on Tuesday morning. For many years he carried on business as a butcher in Butter- market-street, and was one of the oldest tradesmen in Warrington. Mr. Wainwright was 74 years of age and was much respected in the town. PADGATE CHURCH LADS' BRIGADE.

The members of the Padgate Church Lads' Bri- gade who had stayed in camp at Blackpool during the whole of the week returned on Saturday,after- noon. On Friday last the companies in camp were inspected by General Carey. the Padgate Company pining the Warrington St. Elphin's for the inspec- tion. The weather daring the week was rather howery, but the lads thoroughly enjoyed the camp life.

div.head: P.S A. AT THE Y.M.C.A.
div.p: P.S A. AT THE Y.M.C.A.

The Chairman at the above meeting on Sunday afternoon was Mr. Gregson and his remarks were based on "Sowing and reaping." A novel and very interesting address on "Visions and dreams" was given by Mr. Arthur Mounfieid. Miss Kent contri- buted two solos in an excellent manner, viz. : "Sowing the seed," and" He shall feed his flock," from the Messiah. The accompanist was Mr. Hick- man. Mr. H. Barber and Mr. Hedgecock also took part in the meeting.

div.head: RUN OYER BY THE MAIL COACH.
div.p: RUN OYER BY THE MAIL COACH.

William Hill, a middle-aged man, re4iding in Poulton, was, shortly after midnight on Saturday found lying in the road turir the Cemetery. As he was bleeding very much the police ambulance was sent for, and the injured man c9nveyed t 3 the In- firmary. On examination there it was found that he had received a large wound on the head, and several bruises on the body and legs. It is sup- posed that Hill who was intoxicated had either staggered against the mail coach from Manchester to Liverpool, or was lying on the road when it ran over him.

div.head: STRETTON CHOIR TRIP.
div.p: STRETTON CHOIR TRIP.

The annual trip in connection with the Stretton Parish Church choir took place on Saturday, Black- pool being the place selected this year to spend the day's enjoyp3ent at. The choir and their friends, numbering close upon 100, started from Stretton at 5 a.m. in 'buses supplied by Mr. Connor, and were conveyed to Bank Quay Station. Blackpool was reached soon after 9 a.m. The party here dispersed, visiting the numerous places of amusement. The return journey was commenced at 7 p.m., all reach- ing home safely soon after ten. The weather was all that could be desired for the occasion. • SUDDEN DEATH OP A PENSIONER.

An army pensioner named Thomas Turner, 56, years of age, living at 6, Sandy's-yard, Tilley-street, died suddenly on morning Sunday. The deceased had been working in he town as an out-door porter for some time. He had spent the greater part of his time in the army in foreign service, and was subjected to ague. On Wednesday afternoon he complained of pains in his right leg and hip, and went to bed. No doctor, however, was called in, and no medicine was taken by the deceased. He became worse on Saturday night and died as stated.

A IA ARRINGTON PICKPOCKET AT SOUTHPORT. On Monday morning at the Southport Police Court, Joseph Rowley, a Warrington youth, was charged with picking pockets on the shore on Friday. Detective-Inspector Halsall in company with Detectives Howard and Entwistle saw the prisoner put his hand into the pocket of Mies Florence Oddy, a visitor at the watering place, The prisoner denied the offence but was sentenced to one month's hard labour. He was fined ls. for the ft when 10 years of age, and in 1883 was committed for theft at Warrington.
THE WKIIsTLEY TARIFF AND WARRINGTON TRADE.

Inquiriem were made on Tuesday from the War- rington manufacturers with a 'view to elicit what change, if any, the removal of the American impost Upon barbed wire will have. Manufacturers do not anticipate much difference, because hitherto the trade with the Unitod States has been nil. The impost under the Mqiinley Tariff Act was '6 cents per lb., and the removal of this impost will doubt- less cause American manufacturers to reduce their prices so as to prevent any imports from abroad. With regard to iron ore, which has also been freed from duty, Warrington iron manufacturers do nf4 attach any importance to it, becAuse America can manufacture iron cheaper than England.

div.head: TRIPS FROM PADGATE AND ORFORD,
div.p: TRIPS FROM PADGATE AND ORFORD,

On Monday the annual Padgate parish trip took place, wlien a party of upwards of 100 persons journeyed to Lancaster and Morecombe. One por- tion of the party broke the journey at Lancaster, whilst the remainder went on to Morecambe. The weather was threatening,but the excursionists were able to thoroughly enjoy themselves in various ways. Padgate was reached about ten o'clock, everyone being satisfied with the day's trip.—The ' members of the Orford Church Choir, accompanied by a large number of friends, had their annual trip on Monday, when they journeyed to Llandudno. The various places of amusement and interest were visited, and a most enjoyable day was spent.

div.head: ST. ANN'S C'EfIIItCH.
div.p: ST. ANN'S C'EfIIItCH.

The annual choir festivailn--c-onnection with St. Ann's Church was held on Sunday. The pulpit was occupied, morning and evening, by the Rev. James Davies. At the morning service the choir rendered the anthem, "Incline thine ear " (Himmel), Mr. Fred Taylor singing the bass solo with good effect. At the evening service the anthem was " I will sing to Thy power" (Sir Arthur Sullivan), when Mr. H. J, Jenkins, of Holy Trinity Church choir, who was in good voice, rendered the fine tenor solo •.with admirable taste. The services throughout. the day were fully choral, and the singing left nothing to be desired. Offertories were taken .during the day in aid of the choir funds. r-NNIS HEQVISITES.—GARLIND, 51. Bridge-street, War- rington.—Advt. STABLE FIRE AT WHITECROSS WORKS..

On '17;;(-1/Wnight towards ten o'clock a tire broke out in a stable adjoining the Priestly-street side of Whitecross works. Immediately the fire was dis- covered,the works bell was rung, and a large crowd of people attracted to the spot. A number of them at once seized buckets and made every effort to ex- tinguish the fire. Eventually it was found neces- sary to send for the fire brigade, which under the command of Suptrinten(!ent Turner was soon on the spot. Three horses which were in the stable at the time of the outbreak of the fire had been re- moved and were apparently none the worse. The brigade after an hour's hard work succeeding in ex- tinguishing the flames, but not before the roof had fallen in and a large amount of hay and straw had been destroyed. The general opinion was at first that the works were on fire, and indeed this might have been the case as the stable in question adjoins one of the main buildings. For the time it lasted the fire burned furiously, the conflagration being visible all over the town. The cause of the outbreak is unknown. GARDEN SEATS.—GARLAND, Ironmonger, Warrington and Eariestown.—Advt.

div.head: LATE 'MR. SAMUEL BA.RLOW.
div.p: THE LATE 'MR. SAMUEL BA.RLOW.

By final decree made in the action Barlow v. Bolton and others on July 9, 1894, the Court pro- nounced for the force and validity of the will dated September 30, 1889, of Mr. samuel Barlow, of Stakehill, near Cast!eton, and Shinddhu Hir, Little Orme, Llandudno, bleanher, who died on the 28th May, 1893, and declared that the deceased died in- testate as to his residuary estate in remainder in the event of Hannah Elizabeth Bolton dying with- out issue. Probate of Mr. Barlow's will has there- fore now been granted to his wife, Mrs. Hannah Barlow, the executrix for life. The testator be- queaths to his servants Mary Goodard and Mary Monks £5O each ; to his niece Elizabeth Mills a life annuity of 1;52 ; and to Mrs. Barlow £5OO, the policies of insurance, on his life, the plate, pictures furniture, and household and other effects in abut his mansion-house at Little OrmP, the sole and en- tire management of the Shinddhu [Hr estate and the income for life of his residuary estate, which subject. to Mrs. Barb o v's life interest, is to be in trust to pay the income to the testator's niece Hannah Elizabeth Balton for her life, and subject to her life interest the estat6 is to be in trust for her or if she should die without leaving issue then upon such trusts as were declared in a paper

. . . . writing in a sealed packet deposited with the testa- tor's solici tor, but such packet WtIS not to be opened until after the death of the said Hannah Elizabeth Bolton without issue. He appoints his. niece.

Hannah Elizabeth Bolton, and William Bolton, of Warring:on, brewer, trustees. The gross value of the late Mr. Barlow's personal estate has been sworn at £33,019 ss. 10d., and the net value at £29,636 44. 10d.

ANNUAL MEETING OF THE JUVENILE BURIAL SOCIETY. . The annual meeting of toe Warrington Juvenile , Burial Society of the Loyal ()viler of Ancient Shep- herds was held at the Cocoa Rooms, Horsemarket- st.,ou Monday evening,under the presidency of Mr. James Gresty. He was supported by Messrs. William tihlave (vice-president), L. Weir (secretary), James Parr (treasurer), J. Bennion, Eckersley, Whitlow, Dnokworth.Kirkham, Lowe, Jones, Massey,Broady, D. Leigh, Timperley, Harris, Warburton, Miller, Sykes, Holmes, Howard, Cliffe, and others. The secrecary,in presenting the balance sheet and report spoke at some length upon the financial and nu- merical condition of the society. He alluded to the unfortunate coal dispute and the distress and poverty caused thereby. He said spite of all this the past year had been a splendid one so far as the finances were concerned. After paying all expenses there was the handsome balance of £12295. ld.to add to the capital. (Applause.) The present capital is £1,229 53. 411. There had been 22 deaths during the year, out of a total membership of 1128, whiFh had incurred an expenditure of £7l 15s. In passing through the report. he pointed out that the Widr,ws and Orphans' Fund had made again of £4 3. 81. The accounts were certified as correct by the auditors, Niess.rs. Edgar and Jones. The meeting then pro- ' ceeded with the election of officers for the coming year. Mr. Wm. Gleave was elected president, and Mr. T. C. Duckworth vice-president. The secretary and treasurer were re-elected. A long and animated discussion took place as to the advisability of giv- ing the juveniles in connection with the society a treat. It was decided that the matter should be adjourned until the next meeting. Several members spoke rather in favour of a demonstration than a mere treat, and it was thought that during the en- suing twelve months there might be something of that sort forthcoming. A hearty vote of thanks having been passed to the retiring president Mr. James Gresty, the meeting terminated.

div.head: SHIP CANAL.
div.p: SHIP CANAL.

MANCFIES EXPORI'S AND THE CANAL. Thirty-three firms who are among the principal ex- porters from Manchester to China and Japan have signed a document addressed to the China Steamship Owners' Conference, in which they say :—" We think that the time has now arrived when arrangements should be made for us to ship our consignments for China and Japen direct from the Manchester Docks, instead of from Birkenhead or London, and we shall therefore be glad to kow whether the present conference is prepared to supply us with steamers regularly and frequently at Manchester. We would not, in this event, press for any reduction of the equivalent of the through rate of freight during the present year, but would leave the advantage of the saving, which amounts to about 4s. per ton' as compensation to the shipowners for making this new de- parture. In addition the shipewners would reap the benefit of the freedom from ship dues conceded by the Ship Canal Company to ships loaded in Manchesiar dur- ing the next 18 months." Mr. Marshall Stephens, the manager of the Canal.in comnection with this document, states that there is sufficient water in the Canal for any steamer engaged in the China trade. WALTON LOCK. The lock at Walton, for the purpose of connecting the river Mersey with the Ship Canal, is now finished, but before water will be able to run through it, there is a great deal to be done. The approach to the lock at either end is still closed up, but a large gang of men is busily engaged cutting through the river end. In the coarse of a fortnight this will probably be through, and then the river will flow up as far as the lock gates, but no further. Running parallel with the lock is the sluice fnr letting out any overflow of water on the Canal side. The sluice gate itself is now in position and is, in most, respects, similar to the gates at Latchford and other places along the Ship Canal. A good number of men are busy with the work of walling up the banks of the channel, between the Canal and the disconnected portion of the river at Wilderspool. The opening itself has been deepened and widene 1 and when the red sandstone walls are finished it will present mu ch the same appear- ance as its continuation—the Ship Canal.

div.head: F ROBS HAM.
div.p: F ROBS HAM.

A 'TOPER IN THE POLICE COURT.—At the Frodsham Police Court on Monday morning, before Mr. A. Thomas. John Conroy, a sweep hailinv from Oldham was charged with drunkenness in Church-st., Frodsham, on the pre- vious Saturday night and lu the case being proved was fined 53. including costs, or an alternative of seven days' hard labour.

PAINFULLY SUDDEN DEATH.-Dr. Churton, coroner, conducted an inquiry on Thursday, at the Ringro'-Bells, Overton, relative to the sudden death of a man named Thomas Woodward, 56 year's of age. The evidence given showed that the deceased, who had been ailing for a long time, was on Wednesday found in his room in a dying condition by his brother.—The jury returned a' verdict of " Death from natural causes." FUNERAL OF THE LATE MR. WILLIAM HAYES.—The old churchyard of Overton was the scene, on Saturday at noon of a most impressive ceremony, the occasion being the interment of the body of the late Mr. William Hayes, of Ashton Hayes, whose death we announced in our last issue. The funeral procession was met at the gates of the yard by the Rev. H. B. Blogg, vicar, and the ceremony was performed wit' -i much solemnity. The coffin which enclosed the remains, Was of unstained un- turned oak, mounted with bras, and bore the inscrip- tion " William Hayes, born September 7th 1819, died August 7th 1894." Chief among the numerous mourners Were Mr. William Hayes, Mr. F. W. Hayes, and Mr. G. Hayes, (sons) Miss Hayes, (daughter) Mrs. F. W. Hayes, th: Rev. T. Urmston, and some of the deceased's old servants. No floral emblems were seen, it being an ex- pressed wish of the bereaved family that such should not be sent. Although the funeral was of a private nattire a large number ol old friends were present at the graveside amongst whom were Messrs. J. Brundrit, J.P. S. Taylor J.P., T. Handley, J.P., A. Salkeld, J. Ball, James Littler, John Littler,J. Horsefiell, C. A. Timmins, C. Linaker, H. Tiley, S. Gleave, and many others. At the Holy Trinity Church, Runcorn, the Rev. Dr. Preston, vicar, made a feeling allusion on Sunday evening, in the course of his sermon to the departure from this life of Mr. William Hayes. His death would be felt in many directions as the deceased had not lived simply for him- self, but assisted others with an open hand. That. church and pariah had been the recipients of his kind bounty and ready generosity from time to time, but none of these acts were done to get himself talked about, for he was not in the least ostentatious or wishful of praise.
NEGLECTFUL PARENTS AT WIDNES..
SHOCKING REVELATIONS.

On Thursday, at the Widnes Petty Sessions, before Mr. T. S. Timmis and Councillor W. W. Grossage, Daniel Nl‘Derinott, a labourer, living at 29, Elizabeth-street,and his wife, Mary M‘Dernaott, were summoned at the instance of the National Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Children for cruelly ill-treating their three children, Peter, aged eleven, Sarah, aged eight,and John,. aged four, on divers elates between the Ist of June and the 26th ult.—Mr. J. W. Knowles prosecuted on behalf of the society, and in stating the case said the man was, perhaps, morally not guilty, as he appeared to have worked regularly and taken his wages home. But his wife seemed to have spent the money in drink, an when the inspector visited the house he found the woman in a " muddled " state as if from drink. The man had a legal responsibility on his shoulders—to see that his children were not neglected and that they were kept in a proper condition. The society were thus bound to summon him, but they did not ask the bench to send him to gaol; they simpl) wanted a conviction recorded and a fine inflicted in his case.—lnspeetor WAteer deposed to visiting the defendant's house on the 2611 ult., and found Mrs. M'Derrnott there with the three children. The children were very dirty and had vermin on them. They were all without shoes and stockings, and very poorly clothed. The woman herself was in a filthy con- dition, and she appeared to witness as if she were muddled in drink, arid had a black eye. Witness ex- amined the kitchen and cupboard, but could find no food whatever. One of the upstairs reoms was devoid of everything,and in the room where the whole Ad the family slept the only article of furniture was an old iron bedstead, on which was an old tick with straw and chaff. There was no bedding except an old sheet, very dirty. Downstairs, the only furniture wags broken chair and a small round table in the kitchen. Witness visited the house on the 30:h ult., and again on Wednesday, and found the children and house in the same con- dition. Witness believed the man earned £1 per swelc, and the woman admitted that her husband brought home his money. Witness believed that , the man was a sober, hard-working man, but the " ' wife was given to drink, and spent the money.— Dr. O'Keeffe and Police-.4ergeant Carter, who were in company with the inspector, corroborated the evidence of the last witness.—Defendants both gave evi- dence on their own behalf. The man said he gave his wages to his wife every week, and she expended the money on the house. Mrs. 11I'Dermott said the children were fed four times a day, but she had to pawn the furniture to get the food. She denied being drunk when the inspector called.—The Chairman said they were sorry for M•Dermott. So far as they could see he was a hard-working man. He would be fined is. and 6s. 6,1. crsts, but the woman would have to go to gaol for one month with hard labour. •

SUDDEN DEATH. The sudden death is reported to the police of Florence Mabel Reed, ten months old, daughter of Henry Reed, glass bottle worker,4B,Gas-st.,Newton. Tim child died suddenly on Tuesday afternoon from convulsions. No doctor was called in,and the Coron-T has been communicated with, bat it is not likely that an inquest will be held.
INI PER IAL PARLIAMENT.
THURSDAY.

In the House of Commons on Thursday replying to a question. Mr. As4nern said the measures taken in this country for dealing with Anarchists were as well con- sidered and effective for the purpose as those adopted elsewhere, and the Government believed the existing law, administered with energy and discretion, to be sufficient for the protection of the people. Sir WILLIAM flaacounT moved his resolution to appro- priate the whole remaining time of the sessi,on for Government business. Several hon. members put in pleas for their bills. Mr. BALFOUR, who said the CHAN- CELLOR of the EXCHEQUER had given the House the ad- vantage of his services during a laborious and protraetad session, intimated that he should support the Govern- ment. Objection was m tde by various speakers to the agreement between the two front benches and to the treatment of private members. Sir WILLIAM Hai/cobra remarked that if they disapproved of his conduct of the business of the House it was perfectly in their power to dismiss him from a situation for which they thought him unfitted. He promised, after further discussion, that the telephone agreement should not be pressed this session; and Mr. A. MOftLEY subsequently made a simi- lar statement. The House divided, and there were for Sir WILLIAM HARCOURT'S resolution, 130; against, 23; majority, 107. The House then went into Committee on the Indian Budget. Mr. FOWLER, in his lucid statement of the revenue and expenditure of that Empire, said that apart from the lcss on exchange, the whole position of Indian finance was satisfactory and the moral progress of the country was encouraging. It had been urged that the Government should not have interfered with the original intention of the Indian authorities to levy duty on al: imports, ani that the exception of cotton goods could not be justified and was' an injustice to the people of India. But who was going to pay the tax ? The • consumers in India. The House of Commons having declared that the imposition of pro- tective duties on cotton goods could not , be sanctioned, he said, with the greatest sympathy for the Government of India, that the step in the other direction could riot be taken till the House had had some opportunity of discussing the question. The resolution relating to the accounts was passed and reported to the House.

In the House of Lords the Building Societies (No. 21 Bill and the Equalisation of Rates (London) Bill were, after discussion, read a second time. Several other bill were advanced. The House then went into Committee on the Local Government (Scotland) Bill. Ic passed through Committee with amendments, and their Lord- ships adjourned at half-past seven o'clock.

div.head: 6TH V.B. KING'S LIVERPOOL REGIMENT AT CANNOCK CHASE.
div.p: 6TH V.B. KING'S LIVERPOOL REGIMENT AT CANNOCK CHASE.

On Saturday,August 4th, the Newton detachment of the above,consisting of Captain N. McCorquodale and Lieutenant H. S.McCorquodale and 72:rank and tile, left Newton-le-Willows at 11.20a.rn. for Liver- pool,where they joined the battalion under the command of Lieutenant-Colonel Wood, and proceeded by special train, leaving Lime-st. at 12.50-for Rugeley to take part in the Cannock Chase manceuvres. 03 arrival at Elagley Park the men were quickly told off to their tents,and the quarter guard was mounted. In the evening the batta- lion was further strengthened by the arrival of the 7th V.B. Isle of Man Company,under the command of Major Stephen, V.D., and Lieutenant Callow. Sunday At 5 a.m. the reveille was Rounded. Break- fast was served at 7 a.m. The Mersey Brigade 'par:toed for Divine service at 10 a.m. on the Brigade parade ground, where the service was conducted by the Rev. T. B. Harder!)' L.L.D., chaplain-to the corps, assisted by the Rev. G. B. Dicker, M.A., chaplain Ist V.B. Cheshire Regiment. Monday :• The Mersey Brigade (blue) under the com- mand of Brig. General R. S. Shinkwin- took part with the Ist Infantry Brigade • (red) under the command of Major Horsburg,h in an attack and defence practice During the day's proceedings the Liverpool men carried out their part with great spirit, although heavily handi- capped by the rough and broken ground they had to get over, and the fact that through the heavy rain they were compelled to wear- their great coati. The brigade arrived in .camp about 1 p.m. and after dinner, was again formed up to practise movements in perfect silence with a view to carrying out an expected night attack. In the evening- the non-commissioned officers of the 2nd Kings held a smoking concert to which in addition to the non-commissioned officers of the Stafford regiment, representatives of each regiment of ; the Mersey Brigade were invited and enjoyed a most 1 pleasant social evening. Tuesday: The Mersey Brigade (blue) paraded about 8 a.m. and marched to their rendezvous on Etching Hill arriving there about 9.30 a.m. The battle opened by a charge of opposing cavalry, the red being forced to retire by the blue's maxim gun. After a short artillery duel the infantry attack commenced, the firing line being com- posed of the 3rd and 4th Liverpool on the left, and the 6ch on the right. After a stubborn contest with the enemy's infantry, the blue was forced to commence a retirement when " cease fire " sounded. The troops were then marched home arriving in Hagley Park about 1.30 p.m. Wedne,sday : The brigade paraded at- 7 a.m. and marching by an easier route than usual were formed up on the roadside below Bevins' Birches. It was then moved to take up position as the rearguard of an army (red) retiring towards Colwick, which was followed up by a cavalry force (blue) aided by the 2nd Kings and the maxim gun. The cavalry however did little execution on the retiring force, the 17th Lancers in one charge, laying themselves open to a few minutes warm fire from their left. Thursday : After parading at 8 30 a.m.. the Brigade moved off and halting some time at the Cross-roadserear Startley Hill, again advanced to take up position as an advanced guard of the red army advancing from Lich- field, having orders to delay the enemy, and if possible, prevent them passing Jockey Hill till the arrival of the main army from Lichfield :—This, which was mostly an infantry fight, resulted in the red advance guard tieing driven from their position before it could have been supported. The days proceedings ended with a grand march past Major General Julian Hall, and was a • fine soectacle. Sir Redvera Buller (Adjutant General) and Sir Francis Grenf6ll (D.A.G. for Militia Volunteer and Yeomanry), watched the days proceedings and ex- pressed themselves on the whole,very well satisfied with the way the volunteers worked. Friday : In the morning the Brigade was inspected by Major General Julian Hall in quarter column,after which he carefully inspected all ranks and expressed himself well satisfied with the discipline and smartness of the Volunteers. The brigade then marched off.to the Chase to take part in outpost duty.. In the evening the Ml:o's. of the 6th Liverpool entertained their confreres of the line at a smoking concert at which the officers of the corps honoured the 'company with their presence and rendered good service by adding, a few good songs to the programme. Saturday: The various camps were much alive in the morning, preparing to hand over their tents and return to their homes. The special train conveying the 6th Vl3. arrived at Lime-street Station about 12.30 noon, and the battalion at once marched off to their headquarters. The Newton Company arrived at Rules- town at 2.15 p.m.. where under the command of their officers they marched off to Newton, headed by their bugle band and followed by the baggage, On arrival at their store house the company was dismissed—after a few congratulatory words from the captain—to find re- freshments awaiting them. It is interesting to know that Mr. H. S. McCorquodale is the fifth son of Colonel McCorquodale who has served in the Newton Company of what is now the 6th V.B. King's Liverpool Reg!ment, formerly the Liverpool Press Guards.

OVERWORKED TEAMSMEN.—At Sale Petty Sessions 011 Monday ten teamsmen were summoned for being asleep in charge of their horses and lurries. The men are in the employment of farmers resident at Lymm,Timoerley Tat-Am', and other parts of Cheshire, and the offences were committed on various dates when they were re- turning from delivering produce in Manchnter. In every case the defence was Somewhat similar, namely hat the teamsmen had been up all the previous day and night. One youth said he had only had one night's sleep the whole weetr. The Chairman of the bench (Mr. R. H. Joynson) said the magistrates wished they could have the farmers before them instead of the men, as the prac- tice was a most dangerous one. In each case a fine of Ios. was inflicted, and the bench expressed an opinion that the masters ought to pay the money. SUNDAY Scnoot. EXCURSION. —The annual excursion ' under the auspices of the Lymm Sunday Schools took place on Rush-bearing Monday, when a visit was paid to Blackpool. A special train left Broadheath at six o'clock and calling at Dunham Massey and Heatley proceeded to Blackpool. Another' special" conveyed the Lymm,Latch- ford,and Warrington excursionists .Arrived at the popular watering-place the party dispersed, and during the day the various places of interest were visited. The weather was very favourable and all enjoyed the outing thoroughly. The return journey was commenced at 7.25 p.m., and home was safely reached in good time. RUSH-BEARING WEEK.—This week has been generally recognized in the village as a holiday, and most of the principal tradesmen left Lymm for the week. A fair is being held in Mr. John Lee's field, and is well patronised be the juvenile class. On Tuesday afternoon a number of scholars from Latchford visited Lymm, but heavy rain marred their enjoyment. RUNCORN SEAMEN'S MISSION.—On Monday a number of lads in connection with the Runcorn Seamen's Mis- sion paid a visit to Lymm, and held a concert at the Cross. A number of people watched the proceedings, which were of an interesting character, and a collection was made in aid of the mission.

COUNTY OF CHESTER. THE CONTAGIOUS DISEASES (ANIMALS) ACTS, 1878 'l'o 1893. SWINE FEVER. NOTICE IS HEREBY GIVEN, that at a Meeting of the Executive Committee of the Local Authority of the County of Chester, held at Chester Castle, in the said County, on Thursday, the 2nd day of August, 1894. 1. IT WAS ORDERED that from and after the 2011 day of August, 1894, the movement of Swine into the District ot the Local Authority of the County of Chester, from the Counties or places hereinafter mentioned, shall, except upon the conditions herein- after set forth, be absolutely prohibited until this Order is revoked, that is to say Prom the Counties of: Anglesey Glamorgan Buckingham Hants Cambridge Bent Derby Merioneth Devon Middlesex Denbigh Monmouth Essex Montgomery Flint Northampton Gloucester Suffolk or from the District of any separaV, Local Authority situate within any of the before mentioned Counties or places. CONDITIONS— MOVEMENT OF FAT SWINE FOR SLAUGHTER. 2. Fat swine may for the purpose of being slaughtered be moved from a place in the Counties or places before mentioned with a Movement Licence of the Local Authority of the District in which the place from which the swine are to be moved is situate in manner and under the conditions following— (i.) The Licence shall be in force for not more than five days inclusive of the day of issue and shall specify the name and address of the person to whom the Licence is granted, the nuniner and descrintion of the swine to be moved, and the name or description of the place from which, and the premises to which the swine are to be moved for slaughter. (ii.) The swine, before the movement is com- menced, shall be marked by and at the expense of the owner by the painting witki an indelible composition of red colour of a broad line down, the back and another broad line across the loins of each of the swine thus , each line being not less than nine inches long. .(iii.) Before the swine are moved into the District of this Local Authority there must also be a further Movement Licence of this Local Authority. (iv.) The swine moved under this condition shall be accompanied by the Licen&s required thereby, which Licences shall be delivered up to the Police Officer of the County of Chester nearest to the place of their destination by the owner or his agent, within 48 hours after their arrival thereat. (v.) The swine moved under this condition shall be slaughtered within four days after their arrival at the premises specified in the Licence. (vi.) 7he swine while being moved under this con- dition and until they are slaughtered shall be kept separate from all swine not marked for slaughter under this condition. MOVEMENT OF SWINE FOR PURPOSES OTHER THAN SLAUGHTER. x, (1.) Swine may be moved from premises in such he Ce.nties or places before mentioned with a Move- it Licence of the Local Authority of the District in ch the premises from which the Swine are to be red are situate, which Licence shall be in force for more than five days inclusive of the day of issue and 11 specify the name and address of the person to mt the Licence is granted, the number and description he swine to be moved, and the name or description he premises from which, and the place and premises which, the Swine are to be moved, and shall only be granted en a declaration of the owner of the Swine or of his agent authorised in writing for this purpose to the effect hereinafter provided, as to the correctness of , which declaration the said Local Authority shall satisfy themselves before granting the Licence. ' (2.) The declaration shall be to the effect— (a) that the swine to be moved have been on the premises from which they are to be moved for a period of at least twenty-eight days immediately before the granting of the Licence, and that no other pig has been brought on to those premises within such period ; and (b) that the swine are not affected with swine fever, and have not during the period of twenty-eight days as aforesaid been in any way exposed to the infection of swine fever. (3 ) Before the swine are moved into the District of this Local Authority there must also be a further Move- ment Licence of this Local Authority. (4.) The Swine moved under this .Condition shall be accompanied by the Licences and Declaration shall be delivered up to the Police Officer of the County of Chester nearest to the place of their destination by the owner or his agent, within 48 hours .after their arrival thereat. (5.) The Swine shall be moved to the specified place by a route to be prescribed in the Ltcence. The Swine after they are received at the specified place shall be kept isolated for twenty-eight days under the super-. vision of the Local Authority and shall not he moved from that place until after the expiration of that period. REGINALD POTTS, Clerk to the Cheshire County Council. Chester, 13th August, 1894.
